---
title: "In-Game Adjustments, Tempo, and the Sideline Battle"
subtitle: "What coaches actually change between series and at halftime, why some offenses sprint to the line, how defenses answer, and whether the 'halftime adjustments' story survives the data"
description: "How a staff adjusts during a game: the coaching booth, sideline tablets and the between-series loop; what can and can't change in a 13-minute halftime; tempo and the hurry-up offense, the substitution-matching rule and the substitution freeze, and the sugar huddle; a short history of going fast (Wyche's Bengals, the Bills' K-Gun, Manning, Chip Kelly's 2013 Eagles); how defenses answer tempo (simplified calls, rule-based checks, versatile personnel, and the gamesmanship the league polices); the coordinator-versus-coordinator 'call after the call'; and a test of the halftime-adjustment narrative with 2006-2025 nflverse data, including Kansas City's second half in Super Bowl LVII."
glossary:
  "Coaching booth": "The glassed-in coaches' room at press-box level where part of the staff (often one coordinator, quality control coaches and analysts) watches the game from above, sees all 22 players at once, charts what the opponent is doing and relays it to the sideline by headset."
  "Halftime adjustment": "A change to the game plan made during the 13-minute halftime break: re-ranking the calls on the sheet, changing a protection, a coverage mix or who covers whom, or leaning on a play that worked. Almost always a choice from plays already practiced that week, not a new play."
  Tempo: "How fast an offense operates between plays: how quickly it gets to the line and snaps the ball after the previous play ends. Offenses vary it on purpose, from a slow, clock-draining pace to a sprint."
  "Hurry-up offense": "An offense snapping the ball as fast as it can, usually without a huddle, to run more plays, tire the defense and keep it from substituting or disguising. Every team uses it when it is short of time (the two-minute drill); a few use it as a weapon all game."
  "Sugar huddle": "A quick huddle a few yards from the ball, broken almost at once, followed by a sprint to the line and a fast snap: the reliability of a huddle without giving the defense time to substitute or set its own call."
  "Substitution freeze": "The effect of an offense keeping the same eleven players and lining up fast: because the rules protect the defense's right to match only when the offense substitutes, the defense cannot safely change its own players and is 'frozen' in whatever personnel it had on the field."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"

import logging
import os
import shutil
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, RegularPolygon, Rectangle
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, technique, style

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()                # charts: course palette, recessive grid (field diagrams switch their axes off)
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]     # rings on a player to watch: neither offense blue nor defense orange
RED = style.SERIES[7]        # rings on the defender a play is built to punish
GREEN = "#0f7a55"            # darker aqua for text and boxes on the light page


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line(labels=False):
    """Five offensive linemen; unlabeled except the center."""
    names = ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"]
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, w, k if (labels or k == "C") else "")
            for k, w in zip(names, (-3.2, -1.6, 0.0, 1.6, 3.2))]


def spread():
    """11 personnel, 2x2 shotgun: X and Z on the line with the five linemen (seven on the line);
    H (slot receiver) and Y (tight end, flexed into the slot) off the ball."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R"),
                     O("X", "WR", -0.7, -12.5, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -7.5, "H"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 7.5, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 12.5, "Z")]


def tight_12():
    """12 personnel under center, both tight ends attached: five linemen plus Y and U make seven on the
    line; X and Z are off the ball in tight splits."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"),
                     O("X", "WR", -1.5, -11.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 11.0, "Z")]


def flexed_12():
    """The same 12 personnel spread out from the shotgun: both tight ends flexed into the slots (off the
    ball), X and Z on the line with the five linemen."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R"),
                     O("U", "TE", -1.5, -8.0, "U"), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.0, "Y"),
                     O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 14.0, "Z")]


def base_vs_tight():
    """A 4-3 over front with one deep safety against 12 personnel (eight in the box)."""
    return [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "T"),
            D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"),
            D("SAM", "SAM", 3.8, 6.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.8, "W"),
            D("SS", "SS", 7.5, -6.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -11.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 11.0, "CB")]


def base_vs_flexed(lbs_out=True):
    """The same base 4-3 personnel stuck against the flexed 12: the outside linebackers either split the
    difference (apex, between the box and the slot) or stay in the box."""
    sam_w, will_w = (5.6, -5.6) if lbs_out else (3.2, -3.0)
    return [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "T"),
            D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"),
            D("SAM", "SAM", 4.6, sam_w, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 0.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, will_w, "W"),
            D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 11.5, -8.0, "FS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB")]


def nickel_2high():
    """Nickel (4-2-5) two-high against the 2x2: the nickel ($) over H, the safeties at about 12 yards."""
    return [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, -2.4, "T"), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, 0.8, "T"),
            D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.2, "W"),
            D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -7.8, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -12.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 12.5, "CB")]


def cover1_look():
    """Single-high man look against the 2x2: the strong safety down over Y, the free safety in the middle."""
    return [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, -2.4, "T"), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, 0.8, "T"),
            D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.2, "W"),
            D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -7.8, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 7.8, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -12.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 12.5, "CB")]


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="route", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a route, path, run, block or drop."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, pts, frame="field", delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "drop":
        return p.drop(key, end, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=11, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.1, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=11, linespacing=1.1,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=7),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def threat(fld, p, *keys):
    """Dashed brown rings: defenders threatening to blitz before the snap."""
    for k in keys:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, p.players[k].d, p.players[k].w)
        fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.25, fc="none", ec=style.BALL, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (2.2, 1.4)),
                                zorder=7))


def ghost(fld, p, pts, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, alpha=0.55, zorder=5):
    """A faint dashed arrow through absolute (d, w) points: what a player did on earlier snaps."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)), alpha=alpha, zorder=zorder)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                                     color=color, lw=lw, alpha=alpha, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=zorder))


def clean(ax):
    """Zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, and clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, ax=None, width_in=5.8, **kw):
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, width_in=width_in, title=False, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def panel_title(ax, text, fontsize=8.6):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=fontsize, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", pad=3)


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


# ---- frame strips (print) and videos (web) for simulated plays
MARK_R = 0.6    # frame-strip marker radius in yards, smaller than the static diagrams'


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, trails of on-screen players, rings."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.4, play.los + window[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, rr in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"]))
        if rr["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=9))
            continue
        lab = str(rr.get("label", "") or "")
        if rr["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.8 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.6)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.05, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    # once a pass is in the air: the throw as a dashed brown arrow, and a brown ring on the target
    passes = [(k, tt) for kind, k, tt in play.ball_events if kind == "pass"]
    if passes and t >= passes[0][1] + 0.05:
        target, t_rel = passes[0]
        b = df[(df["side"] == "ball") & (df["time"] >= t_rel - 1e-6) & (df["time"] <= t + 1e-6)]
        if len(b) >= 2:
            xs, ys = fld.xy(b["x"].values, b["y"].values)
            ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=8.5)
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=8,
                                         color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, zorder=8.5))
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == target].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.05, fc="none", ec=style.BALL, lw=1.5, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, notes, lateral, window, ncols=2, rings=(), width_in=6.4):
    """Numbered, captioned frame strip: the PDF stand-in for the video."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + 0.55)))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"), fontsize=8.5,
                     color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.4,
                color=style.INK, linespacing=1.15)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=5.6):
    """Web version of the strip: every frame, with the strip's notes as running captions."""
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        cur = [n.replace("\n", " ") for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        ax.set_title(("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (("   " + cur[-1]) if cur else ""),
                     fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), ncols=2):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, notes, lateral, window, ncols=ncols, rings=rings)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=rings)


def canvas(fig):
    """A full-figure axes in 0-100 x 0-100 units for schematic drawings."""
    ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 100); ax.axis("off")
    return ax


def box(ax, x, y, w, h, title, body="", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.1, tsize=8.0, bsize=6.7,
        tcolor=style.INK, gap=3.6):
    """A rounded box centred at (x, y) with a bold title and a smaller body."""
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.3,rounding_size=1.2",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x - w / 2 + 1.2, y + h / 2 - 1.3, title, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=tsize, fontweight="bold",
            color=tcolor, zorder=3)
    if body:
        ax.text(x - w / 2 + 1.2, y + h / 2 - 1.3 - gap, body, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=bsize,
                color=style.INK_2, zorder=3, linespacing=1.22)


def arrow(ax, x0, y0, x1, y1, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.2, rad=0.0, text=None, tx=None, ty=None, tsize=6.4):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw,
                                 connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}", zorder=1))
    if text:
        ax.text(tx if tx is not None else (x0 + x1) / 2, ty if ty is not None else (y0 + y1) / 2, text,
                fontsize=tsize, color=color, ha="center", va="center", style="italic", zorder=3,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load the data: tempo, halftime splits, Super Bowl LVII, the Kelly Eagles)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

# ---------- tempo: game-clock seconds between consecutive snaps when the clock never stopped
TCOLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "play_type", "down", "drive", "qtr",
         "game_seconds_remaining", "half_seconds_remaining", "wp", "no_huddle", "complete_pass", "out_of_bounds",
         "penalty", "timeout", "touchdown", "fumble_lost", "qb_spike", "epa", "success", "ydstogo"]


def snap_gaps(seasons):
    """Seconds of game clock from one snap to the next, on the same drive, when the clock kept running in
    between: the earlier play was a run or a completed pass that stayed in bounds, with no penalty, timeout,
    score, turnover or spike and nothing else logged between the two snaps; both snaps in a neutral game
    state (win probability 20-80%) and more than 2:30 before the end of the half."""
    d = pbp(seasons, columns=TCOLS)
    d = d[d["season_type"] == "REG"].sort_values(["game_id", "play_id"]).copy()
    d["is_snap"] = d["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & d["down"].notna()
    for c in ("complete_pass", "out_of_bounds", "penalty", "timeout", "touchdown", "fumble_lost", "qb_spike"):
        d[c] = d[c].fillna(0)
    prev = d.groupby("game_id").shift(1)
    ok = (d["is_snap"] & prev["is_snap"].fillna(False).astype(bool) & (prev["posteam"] == d["posteam"])
          & (prev["drive"] == d["drive"]) & (prev["qtr"] == d["qtr"])
          & ((prev["play_type"] == "run") | (prev["complete_pass"] == 1))
          & (prev[["out_of_bounds", "penalty", "timeout", "touchdown", "fumble_lost", "qb_spike"]].sum(axis=1) == 0)
          & (prev["half_seconds_remaining"] > 150) & prev["wp"].between(0.2, 0.8) & d["wp"].between(0.2, 0.8))
    out = d[ok].copy()
    out["gap"] = prev.loc[ok, "game_seconds_remaining"] - out["game_seconds_remaining"]
    return out[out["gap"].between(5, 60)]


GAPS = snap_gaps(range(2006, 2026))
G25 = GAPS[GAPS["season"] == 2025]
TEAM25 = (G25.groupby("posteam")["gap"]
          .agg(median="median", mean="mean", q1=lambda v: v.quantile(0.25), q3=lambda v: v.quantile(0.75),
               fast=lambda v: (v <= 30).mean(), n="size")
          .sort_values(["mean"]))
TS = GAPS.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["gap"].agg(mean="mean", fast=lambda v: (v <= 30).mean()).reset_index()
FASTEST = TS.loc[TS.groupby("season")["mean"].idxmin()].set_index("season")
NH25 = G25.groupby("no_huddle")["gap"].median()
WAS_NH = G25.loc[G25["posteam"] == "WAS", "no_huddle"].mean()
NH_Q05 = GAPS.loc[GAPS["no_huddle"] == 1, "gap"].quantile(0.05)      # the fastest no-huddle snaps

# ---------- does tempo work? fast (within 30 s) vs slower running-clock snaps, 2006-2025
GAPS["fast"] = GAPS["gap"] <= 30
YEAR = GAPS.groupby("season").agg(fast=("fast", "mean"), nh=("no_huddle", "mean"))
RAW = GAPS.groupby("fast")[["epa", "success"]].mean()
GAPS["dist"] = pd.cut(GAPS["ydstogo"], [0, 2, 5, 9, 10, 15, 99])


def same_situation_edge(col):
    """Fast minus slower, compared within the same down and distance band, weighted like the fast snaps."""
    cell = GAPS.groupby(["down", "dist", "fast"], observed=True)[col].mean().unstack().dropna()
    w = GAPS[GAPS["fast"]].groupby(["down", "dist"], observed=True).size().reindex(cell.index)
    return float(((cell[True] - cell[False]) * w).sum() / w.sum())


EDGE_EPA, EDGE_SR = same_situation_edge("epa"), same_situation_edge("success")

# ---------- too many men: defensive fouls by huddle vs no-huddle snaps, 2016-2025 (outside the last 2:00)
PCOLS = ["season", "season_type", "play_type", "down", "half_seconds_remaining", "penalty_type", "no_huddle"]
pp = pbp(range(2016, 2026), columns=PCOLS)
pp = pp[(pp["season_type"] == "REG") & (pp["half_seconds_remaining"] > 120) & pp["down"].notna()
        & pp["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run", "no_play"])]
pp["tmm"] = pp["penalty_type"].fillna("") == "Defensive Too Many Men on Field"
TMM_PER_SEASON = pp["tmm"].sum() / pp["season"].nunique()
TMM_RATE = 1000 * pp.groupby(pp["no_huddle"].fillna(0))["tmm"].mean()    # per 1,000 snaps

# ---------- defensive-line rotation: share of defensive snaps per lineman, 2025 (PFR snap counts via nflverse)
sc = nfl().load_snap_counts([2025]).to_pandas()
dl = sc[(sc["game_type"] == "REG") & sc["position"].isin(["DE", "DT", "NT", "DL"]) & (sc["defense_snaps"] > 0)]
dlp = dl.groupby("pfr_player_id")["defense_pct"].agg(["size", "mean"])
dlp = dlp[dlp["size"] >= 10]
DL_MED, DL_80 = dlp["mean"].median(), (dlp["mean"] >= 0.8).mean()
DL_USED = dl.groupby(["game_id", "team"]).size().median()

# ---------- the Kelly Eagles: plays run and faced, 2013-2015
KCOLS = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "defteam", "rush", "pass", "two_point_attempt", "epa"]
k = pbp([2013, 2014, 2015], columns=KCOLS)
k = k[(k["season_type"] == "REG") & ((k["rush"] == 1) | (k["pass"] == 1)) & (k["two_point_attempt"] != 1)]
KELLY = pd.DataFrame({
    "off_plays": k.groupby(["season", "posteam"]).size(),
    "def_faced": k.groupby(["season", "defteam"]).size().rename_axis(["season", "posteam"]),
    "epa": k.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].mean()})
KELLY["faced_rank"] = KELLY.groupby("season")["def_faced"].rank(ascending=False)
KELLY["epa_rank"] = KELLY.groupby("season")["epa"].rank(ascending=False)
PHI_K = KELLY.xs("PHI", level="posteam")
FACED_MED = KELLY.groupby("season")["def_faced"].median()

# ---------- halftime: offense EPA per play by half, team-games 2006-2025
HCOLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "defteam", "home_team", "away_team",
         "play_type", "down", "qtr", "game_half", "half_seconds_remaining", "wp", "epa",
         "home_coach", "away_coach", "total_home_score", "total_away_score"]
h = pbp(range(2006, 2026), columns=HCOLS)
h = h[h["season_type"] == "REG"]
snaps = h[h["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & h["down"].notna() & h["game_half"].isin(["Half1", "Half2"])]
NEU = snaps[(snaps["half_seconds_remaining"] > 120) & snaps["wp"].between(0.1, 0.9)]
LEAGUE_HALF = NEU.groupby("game_half")["epa"].mean()
tg = NEU.groupby(["season", "game_id", "posteam", "game_half"])["epa"].agg(["mean", "size"]).unstack("game_half")
tg = tg[(tg[("size", "Half1")] >= 15) & (tg[("size", "Half2")] >= 10)]
TG = pd.DataFrame({"h1": tg[("mean", "Half1")], "h2": tg[("mean", "Half2")]}).reset_index()
TG["decile"] = pd.qcut(TG["h1"], 10, labels=False)
DEC = TG.groupby("decile")[["h1", "h2"]].mean()
R_HALVES = TG["h1"].corr(TG["h2"])
BOTTOM = TG[TG["decile"] <= 1][["h1", "h2"]].mean()      # the worst fifth of first halves


def persistence(side):
    """Team-season (second half minus first half) EPA per play, and its correlation with the next season."""
    t = NEU.groupby(["season", side, "game_half"])["epa"].mean().unstack()
    t["diff"] = t["Half2"] - t["Half1"]
    t["all"] = NEU.groupby(["season", side])["epa"].mean()
    a = t.reset_index().rename(columns={side: "team"})
    b = a.copy(); b["season"] -= 1
    return a.merge(b, on=["season", "team"], suffixes=("", "_next"))


PO, PD = persistence("posteam"), persistence("defteam")
R_DIFF_O, R_ALL_O = PO["diff"].corr(PO["diff_next"]), PO["all"].corr(PO["all_next"])
R_DIFF_D, R_ALL_D = PD["diff"].corr(PD["diff_next"]), PD["all"].corr(PD["all_next"])

# ---------- points by half and head coach (regulation only)
reg = h[h["qtr"] <= 4].sort_values(["game_id", "play_id"])
fin = reg.groupby("game_id").agg(season=("season", "first"), home=("home_team", "first"), away=("away_team", "first"),
                                 hc=("home_coach", "first"), ac=("away_coach", "first"),
                                 fh=("total_home_score", "last"), fa=("total_away_score", "last"))
half = reg[reg["qtr"] <= 2].groupby("game_id").agg(hh=("total_home_score", "last"), ha=("total_away_score", "last"))
g = fin.join(half)
PTS = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"team": g["home"], "coach": g["hc"], "h1": g["hh"] - g["ha"], "h2": (g["fh"] - g["fa"]) - (g["hh"] - g["ha"])}),
    pd.DataFrame({"team": g["away"], "coach": g["ac"], "h1": g["ha"] - g["hh"], "h2": (g["fa"] - g["fh"]) - (g["ha"] - g["hh"])}),
]).reset_index()
COACH = PTS.groupby("coach").agg(n=("h1", "size"), h1=("h1", "mean"), h2=("h2", "mean"))
COACH = COACH[COACH["n"] >= 100].copy()
COACH["swing"] = COACH["h2"] - COACH["h1"]
PTS["diff"] = PTS["h2"] - PTS["h1"]
SWING_SE = PTS.groupby("coach")["diff"].std().reindex(COACH.index) / np.sqrt(COACH["n"])

# score effects: a team's second-half margin against what its quality predicts. Quality = the team's average
# first-half margin in its other games that season minus its opponent's (first halves start tied, so score
# effects barely touch them); the prediction is the league-wide fit of second-half margin on that quality.
opp = pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"game_id": g.index.values, "team": g["home"].values, "opp": g["away"].values}),
                 pd.DataFrame({"game_id": g.index.values, "team": g["away"].values, "opp": g["home"].values})],
                ignore_index=True)
SE_ = PTS.merge(opp, on=["game_id", "team"])
SE_["season"] = SE_["game_id"].str[:4].astype(int)
tot = PTS.assign(season=PTS["game_id"].str[:4].astype(int)).groupby(["season", "team"])["h1"].agg(["sum", "size"])
SE_ = SE_.join(tot, on=["season", "team"]).join(tot.rename(columns={"sum": "osum", "size": "osize"}),
                                                 on=["season", "opp"])
SE_["quality"] = (SE_["sum"] - SE_["h1"]) / (SE_["size"] - 1) - (SE_["osum"] + SE_["h1"]) / (SE_["osize"] - 1)
SLOPE = np.polyfit(SE_["quality"], SE_["h2"], 1)[0]
SE_["pred"] = SLOPE * SE_["quality"]
SE_["bin"] = pd.cut(SE_["h1"], [-60, -14, -1, 0, 13, 60], labels=["trail 14+", "trail 1-13", "tied", "lead 1-13", "lead 14+"])
SCORE = SE_.groupby("bin", observed=True)[["pred", "h2"]].mean().drop("tied")
SCORE["n"] = SE_.groupby("bin", observed=True).size().drop("tied")
SE_["effect"] = SE_["bin"].map((SCORE["h2"] - SCORE["pred"]).to_dict()).astype(float).fillna(0.0)
COACH["score_eff"] = SE_.groupby("coach")["effect"].mean().reindex(COACH.index)

# ---------- Super Bowl LVII (2022 season): each offense by half, with FTN motion charting
sb = pbp([2022])
sb = sb[(sb["game_id"] == "2022_22_KC_PHI") & sb["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & sb["down"].notna()]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting([2022]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "is_motion"]]
sb = sb.merge(ftn, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"], how="left")
sb22 = pbp([2022], columns=["season_type", "game_id", "defteam", "sack", "play_type", "qtr", "posteam"])
PHI_SACKS22 = sb22.loc[(sb22["season_type"] == "REG") & (sb22["defteam"] == "PHI"), "sack"].sum()
SACK_LEAD22 = sb22[sb22["season_type"] == "REG"].groupby("defteam")["sack"].sum().idxmax()
SB_SACKS = sb22.loc[(sb22["game_id"] == "2022_22_KC_PHI") & (sb22["defteam"] == "PHI"), "sack"].sum()
SB_KO3 = sb22[(sb22["game_id"] == "2022_22_KC_PHI") & (sb22["play_type"] == "kickoff") & (sb22["qtr"] == 3)]
SB_H2_RECEIVER = SB_KO3["posteam"].iloc[0]
SB = sb.groupby(["posteam", "game_half"]).agg(snaps=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"),
                                              rush_yds=("rushing_yards", "sum"), pass_rate=("pass", "mean"),
                                              motion=("is_motion", lambda v: v.astype(float).mean()))


def pct(x, nd=0):
    return f"{100 * x:.{nd}f}%"
```

Second quarter, first-and-10. The offense hits a 20-yard pass, and before the defense's linebackers
have turned around, the quarterback is already standing behind the center, eight seconds after the
tackle, waving his receivers into place. On the defensive sideline you can see the coordinator
frantically waving a fresh defensive back *off*: too late to swap him in. The defense plays the next
snap with the players who were too tired to cover the last one. Twenty minutes later, coming out of
the locker room, the analyst says it: "This game will be decided by who makes the better halftime
adjustments." What actually happens in those two moments? Who decides what, with what information,
and in how much time? And is the halftime story even true?

**You'll be able to:**

- Describe what a staff can change between series and at halftime, who sees what (the
  booth, the sideline, the tablets), and why most adjustments are re-rankings and rule tweaks rather
  than new plays.
- Tell tempo, the hurry-up and the no-huddle apart, explain how a fast offense uses the
  substitution-matching rule to freeze a defense in the wrong personnel, and say how much going fast
  actually gains.
- Explain the sugar huddle and spot it on a broadcast.
- Name the defense's answers to tempo (simplified calls, rule-based checks, versatile personnel) and
  what each costs.
- Follow a coordinator-versus-coordinator sequence, the "call after the call," across a game.
- Judge a "halftime adjustments" claim against second-half data: regression to the mean, score
  effects and possessions.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[The Game Plan: A Week Inside an NFL Building](08-03-game-planning-week.qmd)**: the
  [game plan](08-03-game-planning-week.qmd), the [opening script](08-03-game-planning-week.qmd) and the
  [situational call sheet](08-03-game-planning-week.qmd), the week's menu that every in-game adjustment
  chooses from. In one line: by Sunday the staff has cut the playbook to a few dozen plays, sorted by
  situation, and practiced them; this chapter is about re-sorting that menu in real time.
- Helpful too: the [play-caller](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-caller), the
  [no-huddle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-no-huddle), the 15-second radio cut-off and the staff map from
  [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd);
  [substitution matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-matching) from
  [Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd); the
  [check-with-me](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-check-with-me) from

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and *left* and *right*
are always the offense's. Q is the quarterback, R the running back, F a fullback, Y, U and (once) V the
tight ends, X and Z the wide receivers and H a slot receiver; C is the center (the other linemen are
unlabelled). On defense, E and T are the ends and tackles, S, M and W the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers,
$ the nickel back, CB the cornerbacks and FS and SS the safeties. Solid arrows are routes and rushes,
dashed arrows zone drops (usually with a shaded zone), and a dashed brown arrow is a throw, with a brown
ring on its target. A **purple ring** marks a player to watch, and dashed brown rings mark defenders
threatening to blitz. The blue line across the field is the line of scrimmage and the orange one the
line to gain (the first-down line). The frame strips are simulated plays in Big Data Bowl format, not
real tracking.

## The game is re-planned every series

Start with a fact that surprises most fans: once the game starts, nobody installs anything. The plays
a team will run on Sunday were chosen, taught and practiced from Wednesday to Friday
([The Game Plan](08-03-game-planning-week.qmd) walks through that week). What changes during a game is
the *order* of the menu, the *rules* players use inside each play, and the play-caller's beliefs about
what the opponent is doing. That is still a lot. It's the difference between a chef inventing a dish
mid-service, which never happens, and a chef noticing that table six hates cilantro, which happens all
night.

Two kinds of information drive those changes, and they arrive in two places.

**From above.** The [**coaching booth**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coaching-booth) is the
glassed-in coaches' room at press-box level, the place you met in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd). From up there you see all 22
players at once, including the safeties 15 yards deep whom nobody on the sideline can see. Typically
one coordinator, or an assistant who isn't calling plays, sits there with the quality control coaches and
analysts. While the game goes on they keep running tallies: what coverage did the defense play against
each personnel group, did the safety rotate toward the motion, which blitzes came on third down, which of
our linemen is losing. The league even provides a booth dashboard
for counting personnel groupings and play results in real time.[^booth] It is a coach with a
spreadsheet and a headset, not a genius with a flash of insight.

**From the sideline.** Since the 2014 season every team has had league-issued Microsoft Surface tablets
on the sideline and in the booth. On them, within seconds of each snap, coaches and players get
high-resolution still photos of the formation before the snap and the shape of the play just after
it.[^surface] Under the league's equity rule each team may use only as many working tablets as its
opponent has, so a failure on one side shuts down the same number on the other; the same rule switches
off a team's coach-to-player headsets if the other team's fail
([What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)).[^equity] The pictures are
stills, not video; the point is to answer a specific question ("where was the safety when you released?")
with a picture instead of an argument.

```{python}
#| label: fig-adjustment-loop
#| fig-cap: "Two windows for adjusting a game plan (illustrative; staffs differ). Top: between series, while the other unit is on the field, the booth's tallies and the tablet photos meet the coaches and players on the bench, and the output is small: a rule, an alignment, a protection call, a re-ranked call sheet. Bottom: the 13-minute halftime, roughly how a staff spends it. The bars are a typical order, not a timetable, and the right-hand box is the honest list of what can change."
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 4.5))
ax = canvas(fig)
ax.set_ylim(9, 100)
ax.text(1.5, 97.5, "Between series (the other unit is on the field: a few minutes to a quarter of an hour)",
        fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="top")
box(ax, 13.5, 78, 24, 19, "Booth (upstairs)", "sees all 22 players\nQC coaches, analysts:\ntallies of coverage,\npressure, personnel,\nwho is losing his block",
    fc="#e6e4ef")
box(ax, 13.5, 53, 24, 16, "Tablets", "still photos of every\nsnap, before and just\nafter the snap,\nwithin seconds", fc="#e6e4ef")
box(ax, 47.5, 66, 27, 27, "Sideline / the bench", "coordinator with the QB\n(or the defensive signal-\ncaller); position coaches\nwith their groups, each with\na tablet: 'where was the\nsafety?' 'who had the\nhook zone?'", fc="#e3ecd7")
box(ax, 84, 66, 29, 27, "Output: fixes, not new plays", "• a rule: 'take the inside\n   release away from him'\n• an alignment or leverage\n• a protection call\n• re-rank the call sheet:\n   scratch, promote, save one", fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.OFFENSE)
arrow(ax, 26, 78, 33.6, 72, text="headset", tx=29.5, ty=80.0)
arrow(ax, 26, 53, 33.6, 60, text="photos", tx=29.5, ty=51.5)
arrow(ax, 61.4, 66, 69.1, 66)
ax.text(1.5, 33.5, "Halftime (13 minutes by rule)", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="top")
segs = [("walk in;\ntreatment", 2.0, "#e3ecd7"), ("coordinators meet;\nbooth comes down", 3.4, "#e6e4ef"),
        ("units and position\ngroups: photos,\nwhiteboard", 3.6, "#e3ecd7"), ("head\ncoach", 1.4, "#f3ead2"),
        ("back out;\nwarm up", 2.6, "#e3ecd7")]
x0, scale, yb = 1.5, 4.1, 18.5
for txt, mins, fc in segs:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, yb), mins * scale, 10, fc=fc, ec=style.SURFACE, lw=1.6, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x0 + mins * scale / 2, yb + 5, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK, zorder=3,
            linespacing=1.15)
    x0 += mins * scale
for m in range(0, 14, 1):
    xx = 1.5 + m * scale
    ax.plot([xx, xx], [yb - 1.2, yb], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.7)
    if m % 2 == 0 or m == 13:
        ax.text(xx, yb - 2.6, f"{m}", fontsize=6.2, color=style.MUTED, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(1.5 + 6.5 * scale, yb - 7.2, "minutes after the half ends", fontsize=6.4, color=style.MUTED, ha="center")
box(ax, 81.5, 24.5, 34, 16, "Can change / can't", "can: the call-sheet order,\npersonnel use, protection rules,\ncoverage mix, who covers whom\ncan't: a play nobody practiced",
    fc=style.SURFACE, ec=GREEN, bsize=6.4)
plt.show()
```

The loop in @fig-adjustment-loop runs every time the offense or defense comes off the field. A typical
exchange takes a few minutes and sounds mundane. The booth says the corner is playing inside leverage on
the slot every time it sees trips; the receivers coach shows the slot receiver the photo and tells him to
take the outside release; the coordinator moves a play that attacks outside leverage up his list for the
next series. On defense: the booth notices the offense has run the same crossing concept against man
coverage three times, so the coordinator reminds two defenders of the switch rule they practiced for
it on Thursday.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the booth and the tablets"}
Every play has two halves of information: what the defense *showed* before the snap and what it
*did* after. Players see their own patch of grass; the sideline sees helmets. The booth and the
tablets exist to give the people making the next decision the whole picture, fast. The cost is
attention and trust. A coordinator who tries to absorb everything the booth sees stops thinking about
the next call, so good staffs filter hard: the booth reports only what the play-caller has asked it to
look for, plus anything that has changed. Which coordinator sits upstairs varies by team, which you can
usually spot on a broadcast by who is shown wearing a headset in the press box.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, when a play stops working you scroll to a different one: the whole playbook is always
available. A real team can only run what it practiced that week, and a play that hasn't been repped
against the opponent's looks is a play somebody will run wrong. So "adjusting" in the NFL mostly means
choosing differently from a small menu, and changing small rules inside plays (a protection that slides
the other way, a corner who stops pressing a fast receiver), not drawing up something new in the dirt.
Coaches do occasionally scribble a wrinkle on a whiteboard, but the bigger the change, the more likely it
is to be run badly.
:::

## Halftime: thirteen minutes

The NFL's halftime is 13 minutes by rule.[^halftime] For the staff, that is the one sustained block of the
game in which every coach and player is in the same room, and the coaches from the booth come down to
join them. A [**halftime adjustment**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-halftime-adjustment) is a change
to the game plan made in that window.

Thirteen minutes is less than it sounds. Players need to walk in, get treatment and use the
bathroom; they have to be back on the field in time to warm up; and the head coach usually wants a minute
with the whole team. What's left is a few minutes for coordinators to agree on what they've seen and a
few minutes for each unit to hear the changes. That shapes what a halftime adjustment can be:

- **Re-ranking the sheet.** The plays that worked move up, the ones that didn't get scratched, and the
  constraint plays that the first half set up ([Constraint Theory](08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd))
  get scheduled. This is the commonest and cheapest change.
- **Changing who does what inside the plays already installed.** Sliding the protection toward a rusher
  who is winning, keeping a tight end in to help a struggling tackle, moving the best corner onto the
  receiver who is hurting you, playing more of the coverage that held up and less of the one that didn't.
- **Changing the mix.** More of one personnel group, more motion, more runs, fewer blitzes. The plays are
  the same; their frequencies change.
- **Fixing a tell.** If the opponent seems to know what's coming, a staff looks for what's giving it away
  (a back's alignment, a linebacker's stance) and changes it.
- **Re-planning around injuries.** The most common adjustment of all is forced, and it doesn't wait for
  halftime. When the left tackle or the nickel back goes down, the plan bends around his backup: a tight
  end or back is assigned to help the backup tackle, the protection slides toward him, a backup corner
  gets safety help or is hidden in a package, and plays the backup hasn't repped get scratched.

Notice what's missing from the list: new plays. With five minutes per unit and no reps, there is no time
to teach one.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The second half was won in the locker room." Sometimes the halftime change is real and visible: a
team that was blitzed to pieces comes out keeping six in to protect, or a defense that was gashed by
outside runs starts setting the edge differently. But a lot of what gets called a halftime adjustment
is the scoreboard, the clock and plain luck moving in the other direction, as the last part of this
chapter shows with data. When you hear the phrase, ask: what *specifically* changed?
:::

## Tempo: the clock between plays

Now the other weapon a staff can use during a game: speed. When a play ends, the 40-second
[play clock](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-clock) starts, and the offense must snap the ball before
it reaches zero.[^playclock] What it does with those 40 seconds is its
[**tempo**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tempo): how fast it gets to the line and snaps. Most
offenses, most of the time, use almost all of it: huddle, line up, shift or motion, look at the defense,
snap with a few seconds left. A
[**hurry-up offense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hurry-up-offense) does the opposite and snaps as
fast as it can. Every team hurries when it's short of time (the
[two-minute drill](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd), the subject of
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)).
The interesting question is the team that hurries when it *doesn't* have to.

Three words get mixed up on broadcasts, so pin them down:

- **No-huddle** is about *communication*: the call reaches the players at the line, by signals, words or
  wristbands, instead of in a huddle ([What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)).
- **Tempo** is about *speed*: how much of the play clock the offense uses.
- **Hurry-up** is tempo turned all the way up.

A team can go no-huddle and still be slow (line up fast, then look at the defense and wait for the
sideline), and a team can huddle and still be fast, as you'll see with the sugar huddle below.

How fast do NFL offenses actually play? The play-by-play data doesn't record the play clock reliably, but it
does record the game clock at every snap. On snaps where the clock kept running between plays (the earlier
play was a run or a completed pass that stayed in bounds, with no penalty or timeout), the game-clock
seconds between two snaps measure how long the play took plus how long the offense took to snap the next
one.[^tempodata] A team that snaps with the play clock nearly expired lands around 40 seconds or a bit more;
a true hurry-up offense lands around 25 to 30.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tempo-2025
#| fig-cap: "Tempo by team, 2025 regular season: game-clock seconds from one snap to the next when the clock kept running between them, in neutral game states (win probability 20–80%) and outside the last 2:30 of each half. Dots are each team's average and bars span its middle half of snaps; the number on the right is the share of those snaps that came within 30 seconds. Lower is faster. The league is bunched between about 36 and 40 seconds; New Orleans (orange) was the one offense that regularly pushed the pace. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
t = TEAM25.sort_values("mean", ascending=False)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.5))
ys = np.arange(len(t))
hi = t.index == t["mean"].idxmin()
ax.hlines(ys, t["q1"], t["q3"], color=np.where(hi, style.SERIES[1], style.BASELINE), lw=3.2, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(t["mean"], ys, s=30, color=np.where(hi, style.SERIES[1], style.SERIES[0]), zorder=3)
for y, (team, r_) in zip(ys, t.iterrows()):
    ax.text(45.6, y, pct(r_["fast"]), fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
ax.text(45.6, len(t) + 0.2, "within\n30 s", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="bottom", linespacing=1.0)
ax.set_yticks(ys, t.index, fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlim(28, 46)
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(t) + 1.6)
ax.axvline(TEAM25["mean"].median(), color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(TEAM25["mean"].median() - 0.2, len(t) + 0.5, f"median team {TEAM25['mean'].median():.1f} s", fontsize=6.8,
        color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="bottom")
ax.set_xlabel("Seconds of game clock between snaps (running clock): lower is faster", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

@fig-tempo-2025 says something worth absorbing before any history: the modern NFL barely hurries in normal
game situations. The median team averaged about `{python} f"{TEAM25['mean'].median():.0f}"` seconds between
running-clock snaps, which means it snapped near the end of the play clock, and only one team,
Kellen Moore's New Orleans Saints,[^moore] averaged under 35. No-huddle snaps were faster
(a median of `{python} f"{NH25.loc[1.0]:.0f}"` seconds against `{python} f"{NH25.loc[0.0]:.0f}"`), but not
all no-huddle teams are fast: Washington skipped the huddle on about `{python} pct(WAS_NH)` of these snaps
and still had a median of `{python} f"{TEAM25.loc['WAS', 'median']:.0f}"` seconds. That is the
"information" no-huddle you met in [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd),
and it has a recognizable rhythm: the offense hurries to the line, lets the defense settle into its look,
and then everyone, quarterback included, turns to the sideline for the real call before snapping late
in the clock.

### Why go fast?

If almost nobody does it, why does tempo matter? Because when a team turns it on, at the right moment,
it attacks the defense in five ways.

1. **Fatigue, and the end of the rotation.** Defensive linemen are the biggest men on the field and the
   ones doing the most violent work, so defenses rotate them constantly. In 2025 the typical regular
   defensive lineman played only about `{python} pct(DL_MED)` of his team's defensive snaps, only about
   `{python} pct(DL_80)` averaged 80% or more, and a team used about
   `{python} f"{DL_USED:.0f}"` linemen a game.[^dlsnaps] A rotation needs substitutions, and tempo takes
   substitutions away (the next section shows how), so the same four men keep rushing. At a normal pace
   a lineman gets 30 seconds or more between snaps (@fig-tempo-2025: even New Orleans averaged about 34
   seconds from snap to snap, which is roughly 28 seconds of rest after a five- or six-second play). A true
   hurry-up, snapping 20 to 25 seconds after the last snap, cuts that to 15 or 20 seconds. Tired linemen
   stop winning their blocks and tired defensive backs stop running with receivers.
2. **The substitution freeze.** The rules let the defense match the offense's personnel only when the
   offense substitutes. If the offense keeps the same eleven and lines up quickly, the defense is stuck
   with whoever is on the field. This is big enough to get its own section, next.
3. **Simplifying the defense.** Disguise, pressure and rotation take time: the call has to be signalled
   in, relayed, and then the defenders have to walk to their spots and hold a fake picture. Snap fast
   and the defense has to line up where it will play, which means the quarterback sees the truth.
4. **More snaps.** More plays per game means more chances for a better offense's edge to show up, the
   same logic as a better poker player wanting to play more hands.
5. **Beating the replay.** Scoring plays and turnovers are reviewed automatically, but most other close
   calls, a catch that might have hit the ground or a spot just short of the line to gain, need a coach's
   challenge, and a challenge must come before the next snap.[^replay] An offense that likes the call
   on the field can sprint to the line and snap before the other sideline has seen a replay
   ([Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)).

And the costs, because there are always costs:

- **Your own substitutions get harder.** Changing your own personnel invites the defense to change too and
  slows you down, so a tempo offense tends to stay in one or two groups and needs players who can do
  several jobs: a tight end who can block *and* run routes.
- **Your own players get tired** too, and so do the call and the communication: a tempo offense needs
  short calls, simple rules and a quarterback who can manage the line.
- **The other team gets the ball back sooner.** A fast three-and-out (three plays, no first down, and a
  punt) leaves your own defense on the field after barely sitting down. That last cost turns out to be
  big, as the Eagles film room below shows.

## The substitution freeze

You met the rule that makes tempo a strategic weapon in
[Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd):
[substitution matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-matching). Before the two-minute
warning, if the offense substitutes, the umpire stands over the ball and the offense may not snap until the
defense has had a reasonable chance to substitute too.[^subrule] Here it is from the clock's point of view.

Read the rule backwards and you have the tempo offense's loophole: the protection exists *only when the
offense substitutes*. If the offense sends out the same eleven players, nobody stands over the ball, and
the offense may snap as soon as it is set. The defense can still change players, but at its own risk, and
the risk comes in two forms. If the defense has twelve men in its formation when the snap is about to
come, the officials blow the play dead before it starts: five yards. If the twelfth man is still jogging
off when the ball is snapped, the play runs, and afterwards the offense chooses between the result and
the five yards. That "free play" is why quarterbacks hurry the snap when they see a defender running for
the sideline. Defenses get caught often enough to make the threat real: from 2016 to 2025, outside the
last two minutes of each half, defenses were flagged for too many men about
`{python} f"{TMM_PER_SEASON:.0f}"` times a season, and the foul was about
`{python} f"{TMM_RATE.loc[1.0] / TMM_RATE.loc[0.0]:.0f}"` times as common on no-huddle snaps as on snaps
after a huddle.[^tmm] The result is the
[**substitution freeze**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-freeze): by keeping its
personnel and moving fast, the offense freezes the defense in whatever personnel it had on the field.

Two things set the speed limit. The officials still have to spot the ball and the umpire has to get out of
the way. Only about one no-huddle snap in twenty came within `{python} f"{NH_Q05:.0f}"` seconds of the
previous snap in the running-clock data, and after a five- to seven-second play that is about 15 seconds
from tackle to snap, however fast the offense wants to go. And the defense's call travels the same way the offense's does: the green dot's helmet
radio goes silent at 15 seconds on the play clock, just as the quarterback's does. Against a huddling
offense the defensive play-caller has twenty seconds or more to decide and signal; against tempo he has
maybe eight, starting from the moment his personnel caller (the assistant who watches the offense's
sideline and shouts the grouping) confirms that nobody came on.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sub-timeline
#| fig-cap: "The substitution-matching rule along the 40-second play clock (illustrative timings). Top: when the offense substitutes, the umpire stands over the ball until the defense has had time to match, so the snap can't come early. Middle: with the same eleven players and no huddle, nothing holds the snap back. From the moment the offense is set (the earliest snap), the ball can be snapped at any time, so for the rest of the clock a defense that changes players risks being caught with twelve on the field; usually it stays put. Bottom: the sugar huddle, a quick huddle near the ball, then a sprint and a snap with about 30 seconds still on the clock, against the five or so of a team that huddles normally. The dashed line is the 15-second cut-off for both teams' helmet radios. Inside the last two minutes of each half the umpire does not hold the ball for the defense."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
ax.set_xlim(41.5, -0.8); ax.set_ylim(-0.75, 4.3); ax.axis("off")
OFF_T, DEF_T, HOLD = style.OFFENSE_TINT, style.DEFENSE_TINT, "#e9e7df"


def seg(lane, a, b, text, fc, ec=style.SURFACE, fs=6.2, color=style.INK):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((b, lane - 0.29), a - b, 0.58, fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.4, zorder=2))
    ax.text((a + b) / 2, lane, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color, zorder=3, linespacing=1.05)


def snap(lane, t, text="snap"):
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((t, lane), 1.0, 0.13, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.7, zorder=4))
    ax.text(t - 0.8, lane, text, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.BALL, fontweight="bold",
            linespacing=1.0)


lanes = {3.45: "1. Offense substitutes (huddle)", 2.1: "2. Same eleven, no huddle: the freeze",
         0.75: "3. Sugar huddle"}
for y, lab in lanes.items():
    ax.text(41.2, y + 0.38, lab, fontsize=7.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, ha="left", va="bottom")
seg(3.45, 40, 32, "huddle; new players\nrun on", OFF_T)
seg(3.45, 32, 24, "umpire over the ball;\ndefense matches", HOLD)
seg(3.45, 24, 17, "break, line up", OFF_T)
seg(3.45, 17, 6.5, "shift, motion, look, check", OFF_T)
snap(3.45, 5.6)
seg(2.1, 40, 33, "hustle to the\nline, set", OFF_T)
seg(2.1, 33, 0.0, "", DEF_T)
for xx_, txt_ in ((23.4, "from here on, the snap can\ncome at any moment"),
                  (7.9, "a defense that swaps players now\nrisks 12 men on the field at the\nsnap, so it usually stays put")):
    ax.text(xx_, 2.1, txt_, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK, zorder=3, linespacing=1.05)
ax.add_patch(Ellipse((31.9, 2.1), 1.0, 0.13, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.7, zorder=4))
ax.text(31.9, 2.1 - 0.34, "earliest snap", fontsize=6.0, color=style.BALL, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="top")
seg(0.75, 40, 34.0, "quick huddle\nnear the ball", OFF_T)
seg(0.75, 34.0, 31.2, "sprint,\nset", OFF_T)
snap(0.75, 30.4, "snap with about\n:30 left")
ax.plot([15, 15], [0.3, 4.0], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(15, 4.05, "radio off at :15", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="bottom")
for s_ in range(40, -1, -5):
    ax.plot([s_, s_], [0.0, 0.12], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
    ax.text(s_, -0.08, f":{s_:02d}", fontsize=6.4, color=style.MUTED, ha="center", va="top")
ax.plot([40, 0], [0.06, 0.06], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
ax.text(20, -0.45, "play clock (seconds left)", fontsize=6.8, color=style.MUTED, ha="center", va="top")
plt.show()
```

@fig-sub-timeline also shows why matching matters so much to a defense in the first place. Modern defenses
are built in packages: [base](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-base-defense) personnel with three
linebackers against heavy offenses, [nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel) and
[dime](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dime) with extra defensive backs against three and four receivers
([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)). Each package
is right against some offensive groups and wrong against others. A tempo offense wants to pick the wrong
one for the defense and then keep it on the field.

The classic version is in @fig-freeze. The offense runs a play with two tight ends attached to the line,
a run look, and the defense sensibly matches with base personnel. Then, with the same eleven players, the
offense hurries to the line in a spread formation, both tight ends split out like slot receivers. The
defense can't safely bring in its nickel back, so its base linebackers have to deal with a spread
formation they weren't chosen for.

```{python}
#| label: fig-freeze
#| fig-cap: "The substitution freeze. Left: on the previous snap the offense was in 12 personnel with both tight ends (Y, U) attached to the line, a run look, and the defense matched with base personnel (three linebackers, eight in the box). Right: the same 22 players a few seconds later. The offense kept its eleven and hurried to the line in a spread formation with both tight ends flexed into the slots. The defense can't safely substitute a nickel back, so the outside linebackers (purple rings) split the difference between the box and the tight ends. Now the box has five defenders against five linemen, and each tight end is covered, if at all, by a linebacker in space."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.8))
LAT, WIN = (-16.2, 16.2), (-8.8, 14.6)
p = Play(tight_12(), base_vs_tight(), los=40, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(axes[0], "Snap 1 (huddle): 12 personnel, base defense")
say(f, p, -7.2, 9.0, "two TEs attached:\na run look", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, 11.0, -9.5, "base: 3 LBs,\n8 in the box", fontsize=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
p = Play(flexed_12(), base_vs_flexed(True), los=40, to_go=None)
p.highlight("SAM", "WILL", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(axes[1], "Snap 2 (no huddle): same 22 players")
say(f, p, -7.2, 8.0, "TEs flexed out", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, 8.4, 0.4, "5 in the box", fontsize=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (12.6, -3.5), (4.6, -5.6), "LB on a TE\nin space?", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

Notice what the freeze does *not* do. It doesn't guarantee a good play: base linebackers can cover tight
ends, and many defenses have a call ready for exactly this. What it does is take away the defense's
best tool, choosing the right players, and force the defense to solve the problem with alignment and
rules, which is harder and more error-prone. And the offense gets to choose its moment: tempo is usually a
change-up, turned on after a big gain (when the defense is tired and wants to substitute), or when the
offense sees a personnel group it likes on the field.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the freeze is the matching rule's other half"}
The matching rule's bargain ([Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)
explains why it exists) is that the offense chooses its players first and the defense gets a fair moment
to answer. The freeze is that bargain run in reverse: give up your own right to substitute, and you take
away the defense's protection. The league keeps adjusting the edges of the trade. Since 2025 officials have been told to close the
substitution window if a defense deliberately slow-walks its substitutes, and an offense that fakes a
substitution (a player jogging onto the field and back off to draw a defensive response) now opens a
substitution window, with a warning first and a 15-yard penalty after that. The trigger was a Packers
fake substitution in Week 3 of the 2025 season.[^zebras25]
:::

### The sugar huddle

Between the huddle and the no-huddle sits a hybrid. In a
[**sugar huddle**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sugar-huddle) the offense huddles quickly, a few yards
from the ball instead of the usual seven or eight, breaks almost at once, sprints to the line and snaps
fast. It gets the huddle's strengths (everyone hears the whole call in one voice, the defense can't read
signals) without giving the defense its usual time to substitute, signal its call and set a disguise.
Offenses save it for moments when they have a call they love and want to run it before the defense can
reorganize. Ben Johnson's Lions were known for it at key moments, and Chicago expected him to bring it
with him when he became the Bears' head coach in 2025.[^sugarlions]

You can tell it from a team that merely huddles a little closer by the clock. A normal huddle breaks with
20-odd seconds left and the snap comes with about five on the play clock; after a sugar huddle the
players are in their stances a second or two after it breaks and the snap comes with 25 to 30 seconds
still showing (@fig-sub-timeline, bottom). The huddle itself forms *very* close to the ball, sometimes
with the quarterback facing the line. On the defensive side, watch for defenders looking to the
sideline for a call that hasn't arrived.

## A short history of going fast

Tempo has a richer history than most schemes, because every time an offense used it, the league and the
defenses argued about whether it was fair.

**Cincinnati, 1988.** The first NFL team to make the no-huddle a standard weapon was Sam Wyche's
Bengals, who called it their "attack offense": shortened huddles very close to the line (what today
would be called a sugar huddle), or none at all. In the 1988 playoffs the Seahawks answered it with a
transparent tactic: their defensive tackle Joe Nash went down "injured" on third down after third down,
stopping the clock so Seattle could bring in its nickel package. When Bills coach Marv Levy said he'd do
the same in the AFC Championship Game, the league told Wyche, about two hours before kickoff, that the
Bengals would be penalized 15 yards every time they ran the no-huddle. Wyche, a former NFL quarterback with
a gambler's nerve, demanded the commissioner and threatened to tell the world after the game that the
league's penalties had beaten him. The ruling was reversed within seconds, and Cincinnati won 21–10.[^wyche]

**Buffalo, 1990.** The team that lost that game learned from it. The Bills built their own version, the
*K-Gun*, a no-huddle offense built around three wide receivers and a tight end who could block
and catch (Keith McKeller, whose nickname "Killer" gave the offense its K, by most accounts) and
quarterback Jim Kelly calling the plays at the line.[^kgun] Under head coach Marv Levy and offensive
coordinator Ted Marchibroda, Buffalo went 13–3 in 1990, led the league with 428 points, beat the Raiders
51–3 in the AFC Championship Game, and went on to play in four straight Super Bowls.[^xxv] The K-Gun was
tempo as a *system*: the same personnel all game, the defense frozen in whatever personnel it
started the drive with, the quarterback choosing the play after seeing the defense.

It also produced one of the most famous answers to tempo, which wasn't a defensive scheme at all. In
Super Bowl XXV, the New York Giants kept the ball for 40 minutes and 33 seconds, a Super Bowl record, by
running the ball and sustaining long drives, and won 20–19. The best defense against a fast offense is
an offense that keeps it on the bench. (Bill Belichick's defensive plan for that game, which invited the
Bills to run rather than throw, is drawn in
[The Belichick Patriots](../12-case-studies/12-02-belichick-patriots-game-plan.qmd).)

**Indianapolis and Denver, 2000s–2013.** Peyton Manning's no-huddle was the information version: line
up early, read the defense, and change the play at the line while the defense, frozen in its personnel,
could only disguise ([What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) tells his
"Omaha" story, and [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) his check-with-me
system). When Manning wanted to, he could also go fast: his 2012 and 2013 Broncos were among the quickest
teams in @fig-tempo-history, alongside the 2012 Patriots, who had turned their no-huddle into a true
hurry-up.

**Philadelphia, 2013.** Then came the most famous tempo experiment in NFL history.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tempo-history
#| fig-cap: "Twenty seasons of tempo. Each dot is one team-season's average game-clock seconds between running-clock snaps in neutral situations (same filters as the previous figure); the axis is flipped, so faster is higher. Chip Kelly's teams (orange: the 2013–2015 Eagles and the 2016 49ers) were the fastest in the league in all four of his seasons, and the 2013–2015 Eagles were faster than any other team-season in these twenty years; the 2012 Patriots and the 2012–2013 Manning Broncos (blue) were the next fastest, just before and alongside him (the 2013 Bills, a grey dot near 31 seconds, matched them). The dashed line is the median team. Source: nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2006–2025."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
kelly = {(2013, "PHI"), (2014, "PHI"), (2015, "PHI"), (2016, "SF")}
pre = {(2012, "NE"), (2012, "DEN"), (2013, "DEN")}
key = list(zip(TS["season"], TS["posteam"]))
col = [style.SERIES[1] if kk in kelly else (style.SERIES[0] if kk in pre else style.BASELINE) for kk in key]
size = [34 if (kk in kelly or kk in pre) else 12 for kk in key]
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
jit = rng.uniform(-0.18, 0.18, len(TS))
order = np.argsort([s > 12 for s in size])
ax.scatter((TS["season"] + jit).values[order], TS["mean"].values[order], s=np.array(size)[order],
           c=np.array(col)[order], zorder=3, lw=0)
med = TS.groupby("season")["mean"].median()
ax.plot(med.index, med.values, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_ylim(43.5, 27.0)
for (s, tm), txt, dx, dy in [((2013, "PHI"), "Kelly's Eagles\n2013–15", 0.0, -1.1), ((2016, "SF"), "Kelly's\n49ers 2016", 0.9, -0.2),
                             ((2012, "NE"), "Patriots 2012", -0.3, -0.1), ((2012, "DEN"), "Broncos 2012–13", -0.3, 0.1)]:
    y = TS.loc[(TS["season"] == s) & (TS["posteam"] == tm), "mean"].iloc[0]
    ax.text(s + dx, y + dy, txt, fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK, ha="right" if dx < 0 else ("left" if dx > 0 else "center"),
            va="center", linespacing=1.05)
ax.text(2005.6, med.loc[2006] - 0.35, "median team", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.set_ylabel("Seconds between snaps (faster is higher)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xticks(range(2006, 2026, 2))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2013 (Chip Kelly)"}
Chip Kelly came to Philadelphia from Oregon, where as head coach from 2009 to 2012 his offense snapped
the ball faster than almost anyone in college football, with sideline signal boards and a roster
conditioned to play that way.[^kellybio] In his first NFL season the Eagles went 10–6, won the NFC East
and led the league in rushing.[^phi13] They were also, by a distance, the fastest team in
@fig-tempo-history: about `{python} f"{FASTEST.loc[2013, 'mean']:.1f}"` seconds between running-clock
snaps, with `{python} pct(FASTEST.loc[2013, 'fast'])` of those snaps inside 30 seconds, when the
median team was near 38. They stayed the fastest team in 2014 and 2015, and Kelly's 2016 49ers were the
fastest team that year too.

**What to notice:** the tempo and the scheme were one idea. The Eagles ran a small number of plays
(inside zone and its read-option and bubble-screen packaged plays, the RPOs of
[RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)) from a small number of formations and personnel groups,
so they *could* snap fast and so the defense, frozen and tired, had to defend the same plays with the
same players over and over. On a good day it looked like the defense was a step slow on everything.

**Then notice the bill.** Kelly's defense faced more plays than any other defense in the league in all
three of his Eagles seasons: `{python} f"{PHI_K.loc[2013, 'def_faced']:.0f}"` runs and passes in 2013,
against a league median of `{python} f"{FACED_MED.loc[2013]:.0f}"`. A fast offense that goes three-and-out
sends its own defense back out after a minute of rest. And the offense itself faded. The Eagles' offense ranked
`{python} f"{PHI_K.loc[2013, 'epa_rank']:.0f}"`th in EPA per play in 2013,
`{python} f"{PHI_K.loc[2014, 'epa_rank']:.0f}"`th in 2014 and `{python} f"{PHI_K.loc[2015, 'epa_rank']:.0f}"`nd
in 2015.[^kellydata] Personnel changed a lot in those years (DeSean Jackson was released after 2013 and LeSean McCoy
traded after 2014), so not all of the decline belongs to defenses catching up, but a scheme built on doing
a few things fast is also a scheme that opponents get many reps against: by the third season, every
defense on the schedule had a full year of film on the same handful of plays. The general tools a
defense brings to that problem are the next section. Kelly was let go before the end of the 2015
season.[^kellyexit]
:::

## How defenses answer tempo

A defense facing tempo has a problem with three parts: it can't change players, it has little time to get
a call in (maybe eight seconds instead of twenty), and it has no time to disguise. Its answers go after
each part, and each has a price.

**Substitute first.** The cleanest answer to the freeze is to beat it to the punch: change players the
instant the whistle blows, before the offense is set, as defenses already do with their third-and-long
and short-yardage packages ([Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)).
A defense that expects a hurry-up after a big gain can send its nickel on immediately. The cost is a
guess: if the offense then substitutes, it gets to choose last, and if it snaps while the swap is still
under way, the defense is the one with twelve men.

**Simplify the call.** Every defense that expects tempo has a short list of *tempo calls*: one word, or
one hand signal, that tells all eleven players the front, the coverage and the rush, with nothing that
requires a walk-up, a shift or a disguised rotation. The idea is to be *sound* rather than clever: a call
that has an answer for every formation and every run, so that nobody can be caught out of position. The
cost is plain in @fig-tempo-defense: the defense that lines up where it will play gives the quarterback an
honest picture, and gives up the disguise and pressure tricks of
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)
and [Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: fig-tempo-defense
#| fig-cap: "The same defense with time and under tempo (illustrative). Left, with time: a disguised pressure. Before the snap the defense shows two deep safeties and two linebackers walked up into the A gaps (dashed brown rings), so the quarterback expects a two-deep coverage and maybe a six-man blitz. At the snap the Mike rushes and the Will drops into the middle hole; the nickel blitzes off the edge, and the left end (purple ring) drops into the curl-flat zone the nickel left; the strong safety comes down to the other curl-flat; the corners bail to deep thirds and the free safety spins to the middle third. Five rush, with three deep and three under behind them: the quarterback got a two-high, six-man picture and gets a one-high, five-man play. All of that needs the call in early and twenty seconds to set the picture. Right, under tempo: a one-word call, four rush and a two-high zone (quarters) behind them, everyone aligned where he will play. It is sound against every formation, and it shows the quarterback the shell it will play (quarters defenders still read the routes after the snap, but nobody is pretending)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
LAT, WIN = (-15.5, 15.5), (-9.6, 18.8)
# the pressure look: both tackles in 3-techniques (outside the guards) so the two linebackers can mug the A gaps
mug = {"WILL": dict(d=2.2, w=-1.0), "MIKE": dict(d=2.2, w=1.0), "LDT": dict(w=-2.4), "RDT": dict(w=2.4),
       "NB": dict(d=3.0, w=-7.4)}
mug = [q.moved(**mug[q.key]) if q.key in mug else q for q in nickel_2high()]
p = Play(spread(), mug, los=35, to_go=None)
for k_ in ("LDT", "RDT", "RDE", "MIKE"):
    p.rush(k_)
p.rush("NB", pts=[(-3.2, 1.0), (-8.0, 4.6)])
# three under: the dropping end replaces the blitzing nickel in the curl-flat, the Will takes the hole
p.drop("LDE", (6.5, -8.5), zone=(4, 5)); p.drop("WILL", (7.0, -0.5), zone=(4, 5)); p.drop("SS", (7.5, 7.0), zone=(4, 5))
# three deep: the corners bail to the outside thirds, the free safety spins to the middle third
p.drop("LCB", (14.5, -12.0), zone=(4, 6)); p.drop("RCB", (14.5, 12.0), zone=(4, 6)); p.drop("FS", (14.5, 0.0), zone=(4, 7))
p.highlight("LDE", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
threat(f, p, "MIKE", "WILL")
panel_title(axes[0], "With time: show one thing, play another")
point_to(f, p, (4.8, 4.6), (2.2, 1.0), "M rushes", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.0)
point_to(f, p, (10.6, -4.4), (6.2, -0.8), "W drops", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.0)
say(f, p, 3.4, 11.2, "two-high look,\nspins to one", fontsize=6.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
p = Play(spread(), nickel_2high(), los=35, to_go=None)
for k_ in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE"):
    p.rush(k_)
p.drop("LCB", (13.5, -11.0), zone=(6, 6)); p.drop("FS", (13.0, -4.0), zone=(6, 6))
p.drop("SS", (13.0, 4.0), zone=(6, 6)); p.drop("RCB", (13.5, 11.0), zone=(6, 6))
p.drop("NB", (6.0, -8.5), zone=(4, 5)); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -2.5), zone=(4, 5)); p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 3.5), zone=(4, 5))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(axes[1], "Under tempo: one word, no disguise")
say(f, p, -6.6, 8.6, "4 rush, quarters:\nwhat you see is\nwhat you get", fontsize=6.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

**Let the players adjust by rule.** The defensive version of a
[check-with-me](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-check-with-me) is a call that isn't finished until the
offense lines up: the sideline sends a front and a coverage family, and the players finish it themselves
according to the formation they see (set the strength to the tight end, play quarters against two
receivers on a side and a different rule against three). The [green-dot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-green-dot) linebacker or the safeties
communicate the finishing touches with one or two words. This moves the decision from the coordinator,
who is now too slow, to the players. The price is practice time and brainpower: every rule has to be
repped against every formation during the week, a single player who gets the rule wrong breaks the
coverage, and a defense built on rules is predictable to an offense that has studied them.

**Recruit players who don't need to come off.** The deepest answer is roster construction. If your
"linebacker" can cover a slot receiver and your nickel back can fit a run like a linebacker, the
freeze stops hurting, because your base defense and your nickel defense are the same eleven men. The
league-wide rise of hybrid safety-linebackers and the
[big nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-big-nickel) (a third safety as the fifth defensive
back) is partly a response to tempo and spread offenses: it's the defense's way of buying back the
substitution the freeze took away. The price here is size and scarcity. A 210-pound hybrid who can
cover a slot receiver gets moved by a 315-pound guard when the offense runs at him, and a linebacker big
enough to take on that guard usually can't run with a receiver. Players who can do both are rare, and
expensive.

**Slow the game down.** And then there are the answers the league polices. The 1988 Seahawks' fake
injuries were not the last: in September 2011, after two Giants defenders went down at the same moment
against the Rams' no-huddle on *Monday Night Football*, the league sent every team a memo warning of
fines, suspensions and even lost draft picks for faking injuries.[^giants11] The rules add a cost of their
own: before the two-minute warning, a player whose injury stops the game must leave for at least one
down,[^injury] so a fake costs the defense the faker. Defenses can also take a timeout, the cleanest
reset there is, if they're willing to spend it. In college football, where tempo became far more
extreme, the rules committee in 2014 proposed a ten-second window at the start of each play clock in
which the offense couldn't snap, to let defenses substitute. It drew loud opposition from tempo coaches
and was shelved.[^ncaa10]

```{python}
#| label: fig-tempo-snap
#| fig-cap: "Tempo catching a defense unset (simulated, BDB-format tracking). The defense's call is a perfectly good one: a two-high nickel look (quarters behind four rushers), with the nickel ($, purple ring) to line up over H, the slot receiver. Panel 1: the offense, which kept its personnel after the last play, is set two seconds before the snap while the defense is still getting the call and moving into place: the cornerback is jogging out to X and the nickel is still well inside, walking toward H. Panel 2: a second before the snap, the nickel is still a few yards inside H. Panel 3: the snap comes while he is moving, inside H's shoulder. Panel 4: H breaks to the outside, away from him, and the ball (dashed brown arrow) arrives on H (brown ring) before the nickel can recover.
```
