Nothing about the call was wrong; the defense simply never got lined up to play it."
```{python}
def tempo_play():
    dfn = nickel_2high()
    start = {"LCB": (8.5, -6.0), "NB": (6.8, -2.0), "WILL": (4.2, 0.6), "FS": (8.0, -3.5),
             "MIKE": (4.0, 4.0), "SS": (9.0, 4.5)}
    end = {"LCB": (7.0, -12.5), "NB": (5.4, -5.0), "WILL": (4.6, -2.4), "FS": (11.0, -7.0),
           "MIKE": (4.6, 1.8), "SS": (11.5, 7.5)}
    dfn = [q.moved(d=start[q.key][0], w=start[q.key][1]) if q.key in start else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=45, to_go=10)
    for k_, spd in (("LCB", 2.9), ("NB", 1.45), ("WILL", 1.3), ("FS", 2.0), ("MIKE", 1.0), ("SS", 1.5)):
        p.motion(k_, to=end[k_], speed=spd)
    p.route("H", [(0, 0), (3.0, 0.0), (3.4, 4.0)], side=-1)
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (12.0, 0.0)], side=-1)
    p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (6.0, 0.0), (6.0, -3.0)])
    p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (10.0, 0.0)])
    p.dropback(1.5)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.4, -1.4)])
    for k_ in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k_, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
    for k_ in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k_, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "NB", (3.2, -7.4), "path", delay=0.45, speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "LCB", (10.0, -11.4), "path", speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (5.5, -4.0), "path", delay=0.2, speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.5, 2.5), "path", delay=0.2, speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "RCB", (9.5, 12.5), "path", delay=0.2, speed=3.0)     # backpedal with Z
    go_to(p, "SS", (13.0, 8.5), "path", delay=0.2, speed=1.8)      # shuffle out over the top
    go_to(p, "FS", (12.5, -7.5), "path", delay=0.2, speed=1.6)
    p.pass_to("H", t=0.7)
    return p


animation_or_strip(tempo_play(), [-2.0, -0.8, 0.0, 1.4],
                   ["offense set; defense\nstill moving in", "nickel still inside H", "snap: $ is moving,\ninside H",
                    "H breaks out, away from $;\nthe throw arrives on rhythm"],
                   lateral=(-17.0, 14.5), window=(-7.5, 15.0), rings=(("NB", PURPLE),))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
When an offense goes fast, take your eyes off the ball for one snap and watch the defense's sideline
and its secondary. Is anyone running *off* the field as the ball is snapped? Is a defender still
pointing or walking to his spot? Is the defense lining up in a plain look it hasn't shown all day? Those
are the costs of tempo being paid, and they tell you why the offense chose that moment.
:::

## Does tempo work, and why did it fade?

The obvious question about all of this: does going fast actually gain yards? The running-clock data can
give a rough answer. Of the snaps in @fig-tempo-2025's sample from 2006 to 2025, call a snap "fast" if it
came within 30 seconds of the previous one. Fast snaps averaged
`{python} f"{RAW.loc[True, 'epa']:+.3f}"` [EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) per play and a
`{python} pct(RAW.loc[True, 'success'])` [success rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate),
against `{python} f"{RAW.loc[False, 'epa']:+.3f}"` and `{python} pct(RAW.loc[False, 'success'])` for the rest
(@fig-tempo-work, right). Part of that gap is the situation, not the speed: fast snaps are more often
second- or third-and-short, where every offense does well. Comparing only snaps on the same down and a
similar distance shrinks the edge to about `{python} f"{EDGE_EPA:+.2f}"` EPA per play and
`{python} f"{100 * EDGE_SR:.1f}"` points of success rate.[^tempowork]

So tempo works, a little, *as it is used*. That last phrase matters. Offenses go fast when they like what
they see (a tired defense, a mismatch frozen on the field), so this measures tempo at the moments a
play-caller chose, not what would happen if a team snapped fast every time. An edge of three hundredths of
a point per play is worth having on the snaps you pick; it is not big enough to pay the bill Kelly's
defenses paid if you go fast all game.

That may be why the league tried tempo and then mostly put it back on the shelf. In the left panel, the
share of fast snaps rose from about one in twelve in the late 2000s to about one in seven in Kelly's years,
then drifted back. Three things probably explain the retreat. The bill is real: a fast offense that stalls
puts its own defense back on the field. Defenses found the answers in the previous section, above all the
versatile players who make the freeze hurt less. And the style of offense that took over uses the play
clock instead of racing it: pre-snap shifts and motion, which take seconds every snap, rose from 37.6% of
plays in 2014 to 63.9% in 2025 by PFF's charting,[^pffmotion] and an offense that changes personnel
groups from play to play opens the matching window every time it does
([Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)). Going fast survives as a
change-up, which is what the data says it is good for.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tempo-work
#| fig-cap: "Does tempo work? Running-clock snaps in neutral situations, regular seasons 2006–2025 (same filters as the tempo chart). Left: the share of snaps that came within 30 seconds of the previous one, and the share run without a huddle, by season. Both rose to a peak in Chip Kelly's Eagles years (shaded) and then fell back. Right: EPA per play on fast snaps and on the rest. The raw gap (bars) is partly situation; comparing the same down and distance leaves an edge of about three hundredths of a point per play. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.9), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.7, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
ax.axvspan(2012.5, 2015.5, color=style.SERIES[1], alpha=0.12, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.plot(YEAR.index, YEAR["fast"], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.8, marker="o", ms=3, label="within 30 s", zorder=3)
ax.plot(YEAR.index, YEAR["nh"], color=style.SERIES[2], lw=1.8, marker="o", ms=3, label="no huddle", zorder=3)
ax.text(2014, 0.197, "Kelly's\nEagles", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="top", linespacing=1.0)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.2)
ax.set_yticks([0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20])
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xticks(range(2006, 2026, 3))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.set_title("Share of running-clock snaps", fontsize=8.2)
ax.legend(fontsize=6.6, loc="lower right", frameon=False)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax = axes[1]
vals = [RAW.loc[True, "epa"], RAW.loc[False, "epa"]]
ax.bar([0, 1], vals, width=0.55, color=[style.SERIES[1], style.BASELINE], zorder=3)
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(i, v + 0.002, f"{v:+.3f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ["within\n30 s", "slower"], fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.075)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6.8)
ax.set_title("EPA per play", fontsize=8.2)
ax.text(0.5, 0.071, f"same down & distance:\nedge {EDGE_EPA:+.2f}", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="top")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

## The call after the call

Everything so far has been about each side adjusting to what the other *did*. The best play-callers go one
step further and call for what the other side is *about to do*. That is the coordinator-versus-coordinator
contest that coaches sometimes call "the call after the call": you don't call the play that beats what
the defense just ran; you call the play that beats what the defense will run *in response* to what you just
did.

@fig-call-ladder is a small, illustrative version over one half. Each box is an answer to the box before
it, and each side is trying to stay a move ahead.

```{python}
#| label: fig-call-ladder
#| fig-cap: "The call after the call (illustrative, one half). Read the boxes in order, zig-zagging between the offense's play-caller (left) and the defense's (right). Each call answers the last answer. The offense opens by attacking its three-receiver side; the defense rotates its coverage there; the offense punishes the side the rotation left; the defense helps on that side; the offense goes back to the side that has lost its help (and, with three defenders spread out over the trips receivers and a safety committed to X, runs at a light box); the defense starts disguising which one it's playing; and the offense uses motion to make the defense show its hand before the snap. Every step is a play from the week's plan; what changes is the order."
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 6.2))
ax = canvas(fig)
ax.text(24, 97.5, "Offense's play-caller", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(76, 97.5, "Defense's play-caller", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ha="center", va="top")
steps = [
    ("L", 86, "1. Attack the trips side", "three receivers to one side: a quick\nconcept against three defenders"),
    ("R", 75, "2. Rotate to the trips", "the safety spins toward the three\nreceivers: four defenders on three"),
    ("L", 62, "3. Isolate the backside", "the lone receiver (X) now has a corner\nwith no help: slant, dig, back-shoulder"),
    ("R", 51, "4. Help on X", "the backside safety stays over X (a\nbracket); trips side plays three-on-three"),
    ("L", 38, "5. Back to the trips side", "3-on-3 with no help: a rub or flood; and with\n3 out on the trips and a safety over X, the\nbox is light: run"),
    ("R", 27, "6. Disguise which one", "show the bracket, play the rotation\n(or the reverse) to make the read a guess"),
    ("L", 14, "7. Make them show it", "motion before the snap: whoever follows\ntells the QB which coverage it is; check"),
]
pos = {}
for side, y, t_, b_ in steps:
    x = 24 if side == "L" else 76
    ec = style.OFFENSE if side == "L" else style.DEFENSE
    fc = style.OFFENSE_TINT if side == "L" else style.DEFENSE_TINT
    box(ax, x, y, 44, 10.5, t_, b_, fc=fc, ec=ec, bsize=6.5)
    pos[t_[:2]] = (x, y)
ys_ = [s[1] for s in steps]
for i in range(len(steps) - 1):
    (s0, y0, *_), (s1, y1, *_) = steps[i], steps[i + 1]
    x0 = 46.5 if s0 == "L" else 53.5
    x1 = 53.5 if s1 == "R" else 46.5
    arrow(ax, x0, y0 - 2.0, x1, y1 + 2.0, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.1)
ax.text(50, 3.2, "Each call is chosen to beat the answer it expects next, not the last play.",
        fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center", style="italic",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc="#f3ead2", ec="none"))
plt.show()
```

A few things make this contest more than rock-paper-scissors.

**Both sides keep score.** The booth's tallies are not just for the play-caller's own side. The offensive
staff is also tracking the defense's *answers*: when we showed trips, what did they do; when we
motioned, who followed. After a couple of series, each staff has a little in-game tendency report on the
other, the live version of the self-scouting and tendency work in
[Constraint Theory](08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd).

**The second answer is often the money call.** A play-caller can deliberately run a play he expects the
defense to adjust to, *in order to* set up the play that beats the adjustment. That's the sequencing idea
from [Constraint Theory](08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd) applied across a game, and the reason
the most dangerous moment for a defense is often right after it has fixed a problem.

**Nobody can go infinitely deep.** If the offense calls for the defense's adjustment, the defense can
skip the adjustment and stay where it was, and now the offense's clever call is running into the very
defense it was designed to avoid. In practice coordinators think about one or two moves ahead, and
the deciding factor is usually what the players can execute. A defense with one coverage it plays brilliantly
can ignore much of this contest; a defense with five it plays adequately is always one step from a bust.

Here is a single adjustment and its answer as frame pairs. In the first half the defense plays man
coverage on third down, and the offense beats it repeatedly with
[mesh](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mesh), two shallow crossers that run past each other so the
defenders chasing them in man have to fight through traffic. At halftime the defense keeps the same look
but changes the rule for the two inside defenders: instead of each chasing one crosser all the way across
the field, each sits in his area and takes whichever crosser comes to him, a
[banjo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-banjo)-style "pass it off" rule (a
[combo coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-combo-coverage)).

```{python}
#| label: fig-before-after
#| fig-cap: "A halftime adjustment as frame pairs (simulated, BDB-format tracking; illustrative). Each row shows the same third-and-7 play at the snap and 2.3 seconds later. Top, first half: man coverage behind a six-man rush (both linebackers blitz; the back stays in to block). H (from the left, at about five yards) and Y (from the right, a yard deeper) cross over the ball. The nickel ($) chasing H and the strong safety (SS) chasing Y each have to get through the other crosser, so each ends up a step or two behind his man; H is open as he clears the traffic and the ball (dashed brown arrow) is already on its way to him. Bottom, second half: the same look, the same six rushers and the same play, but the two inside defenders (purple rings) no longer chase. Each sits at five to six yards in his own area and takes whichever crosser comes to him: the nickel takes Y, the strong safety takes H, and each crosser runs straight at a waiting defender. The play didn't change; one rule did."
def mesh(second_half):
    p = Play(spread(), cover1_look(), los=55, to_go=7)
    # mesh: two crossers about a yard apart in depth (H under at 4.5-5, Y over at 5.5-6), meeting over the ball
    go_to(p, "H", (5.0, 12.0), "route", via=[(4.4, -5.5)])
    go_to(p, "Y", (6.1, -12.0), "route", via=[(5.6, 5.5)])
    go_to(p, "X", (15.0, -13.0), "route"); go_to(p, "Z", (15.0, 13.0), "route")
    p.dropback(1.5)
    for k_ in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k_, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, 1.0)])
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("RCB", "Z")
    go_to(p, "FS", (15.0, 0.0), "drop", speed=1.5)
    for k_ in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k_, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (0.4, 2.4), "path", speed=3.0)     # right B gap (the tackle has the right A gap)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (0.6, -0.8), "path", speed=3.0)    # left A gap
    if not second_half:
        # man: each chaser trails his crosser by a step or two, on his hip, and loses ground in the traffic
        go_to(p, "NB", (4.9, 3.6), "path", via=[(4.6, -5.6), (4.5, -1.4)], speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "SS", (6.3, -3.4), "path", via=[(6.2, 5.6), (6.3, 1.6)], speed=4.4)
        p.pass_to("H", t=1.75)
    else:
        # banjo: each sits in his area and takes whichever crosser comes to him
        go_to(p, "NB", (6.3, -6.6), "path", speed=2.4)
        go_to(p, "SS", (4.9, 6.6), "path", speed=2.4)
    return p


LAT, WIN = (-16.0, 16.0), (-7.8, 18.2)
T2 = 2.3
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.4, 5.9))
for row, sh in enumerate((False, True)):
    p = mesh(sh)
    df = tracking(p)
    rings = (("NB", PURPLE), ("SS", PURPLE)) if sh else ()
    for col, t in enumerate((0.0, T2)):
        ax = axes[row, col]
        f = panel(ax, p, df, t, LAT, WIN, rings=rings)
        half = "Second half" if sh else "First half"
        ax.set_title(f"{half}: " + ("snap" if t == 0 else f"+{t:.1f} s"), fontsize=8.4, color=style.INK, loc="left",
                     fontweight="bold")
        if col == 1:
            hd, hw = p.position("H", t)
            yd, yw = p.position("Y", t)
            if not sh:
                say(f, p, 12.0, -6.5, "man: each chaser\na step behind", fontsize=6.3, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
                say(f, p, hd + 3.0, hw + 2.6, "H open", fontsize=6.3, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
            else:
                point_to(f, p, (12.0, -8.5), (6.3, -6.6), "$ takes Y", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.3)
                point_to(f, p, (12.0, 9.0), (4.9, 6.6), "SS takes H", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.3)
                say(f, p, -5.6, 9.5, "nobody open", fontsize=6.3, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        else:
            say(f, p, 10.0, -9.0, "same look\nboth halves", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The second-half picture in @fig-before-after looks like a win for the defense, and for a series or two it
is. But every fix gives something away, and this one does too: the two inside defenders now *stop* and
wait. What that hands the offense is the next call after the call, and you'll get to make it yourself in
the second drill at the end of the chapter.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the same pair from real tracking data"}
With Big Data Bowl tracking data you can build @fig-before-after from real plays: find two snaps from
the same game, the same offense and a similar look, one from each half, and draw each at the snap and a
couple of seconds later. The online version of this chapter includes a short code sketch that does it
with `gridiron.bdb` (it isn't run here, because the tracking files are a separate download from Kaggle). The 2025 edition's files cover weeks 1–9
of the 2022 season, with pre-snap frames included ([Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)).
:::

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the real-data version: one play from each half of the same game)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, frame_strip

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")        # Big Data Bowl 2025 files (2022 season, weeks 1-9)
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
game = plays[plays["gameId"] == 2022091100]                       # pick a game
third = game[(game["down"] == 3) & (game["passResult"].notna())]
first_half = third[third["quarter"] <= 2].iloc[0]
second_half = third[third["quarter"] >= 3].iloc[0]
for row in (first_half, second_half):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=row["gameId"], play_id=row["playId"])
    frame_strip(one, times=[0.0, 2.3], title=f"Q{row['quarter']}: {row['pff_passCoverage']}")
```

## Do halftime adjustments decide games? Testing the narrative

Back to the analyst's line. If halftime adjustments decide games, three things should show up in the data:
second halves should look different from first halves in a way that favors the team with the better
staff; a team's first-half performance shouldn't tell you much about its second half (the adjustment
breaks the pattern); and some coaches should be consistently better than others at turning a game around
after halftime. The play-by-play data lets us check each one. All the numbers below use regular-season
games from 2006 to 2025 and leave out the last two minutes of each half and snaps where one team's
[win probability](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-win-probability) (a model's estimate of each team's
chance of winning from that moment, built in
[Win Probability and Decision Analysis](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd))
was above 90%, so that two-minute drills and garbage time (the late minutes of a lopsided game, which
analysts [filter out](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-garbage-time-filter)) don't dominate.[^halfdata]

**First: second halves look exactly like first halves, on average.** League-wide, offenses averaged
`{python} f"{LEAGUE_HALF['Half1']:+.3f}"` EPA per play in first halves and
`{python} f"{LEAGUE_HALF['Half2']:+.3f}"` in second halves. If defenses (or offenses) systematically
out-adjusted the other side at halftime, you'd expect a gap. There isn't one, which is what you'd expect if
both sides adjust about equally well, and if most adjusting happens every series rather than once.

**Second: the first half tells you very little about the second half, and that's mostly not adjustment.**
@fig-halftime-test (left) splits about `{python} f"{len(TG):,}"` team-games by how well each offense played in
the first half. Offenses that were terrible before halftime were much better after it, and offenses that
were brilliant came back to earth. The correlation between a team's first-half and second-half EPA per
play in the same game is only `{python} f"{R_HALVES:.2f}"`, on a scale where 0 means the first half tells
you nothing about the second and 1 means it tells you everything.

That looks like a story about adjustments, and it's the classic trap of
*regression to the mean*. A first half is about 25 to 35 snaps, and EPA per play over that few snaps is
mostly noise: a fumble, a dropped pass, a 60-yard run. An offense that had an awful first half was
usually an ordinary offense having an unlucky half, and its next half looks ordinary, *whether or not
anyone adjusted anything*. The team that "came out a different team after halftime" was often just the
same team without the bad bounces. The same arithmetic makes the hot first-half team cool off.

```{python}
#| label: fig-halftime-test
#| fig-cap: "Testing the halftime narrative, 2006–2025 regular seasons (neutral snaps). Left: team-games grouped into tenths by the offense's first-half EPA per play; each dot is a group's average first half (x) against its second half (y). If the first half carried over, the dots would lie on the dashed diagonal; instead they lie almost flat: bad first halves were followed by about average second halves, and great ones too. That is regression to the mean, not proof of adjustment. Right: is 'improving after halftime' a team trait? Each dot is a team-season's second-half minus first-half EPA per play, plotted against the same team's number the next season. There is essentially no relationship (r near zero), while a team's overall EPA per play carries over from one season to the next quite strongly (r about 0.4). Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.2))
ax = axes[0]
lim = (-0.62, 0.55)
ax.plot(lim, lim, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
ax.plot(DEC["h1"], DEC["h2"], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(DEC["h1"], DEC["h2"], s=26, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3)
ax.set_xlim(*lim); ax.set_ylim(*lim)
ax.set_xlabel("First-half EPA per play", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Second-half EPA per play", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_title("A bad first half, then an average second", fontsize=8.4)
ax.text(0.12, 0.33, "if the first half\ncarried over", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center")
ax.annotate("worst tenth of\nfirst halves", (DEC["h1"].iloc[0], DEC["h2"].iloc[0]), xytext=(-0.42, 0.24),
            fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax = axes[1]
ax.scatter(PO["diff"], PO["diff_next"], s=9, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.45, lw=0, zorder=2)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1); ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
ax.set_xlim(-0.32, 0.32); ax.set_ylim(-0.32, 0.32)
ax.set_xlabel("2nd-half minus 1st-half EPA/play, season N", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Same, season N+1", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_title("'Second-half team' is not a trait", fontsize=8.4)
ax.text(0.30, -0.24, f"r = {R_DIFF_O:.2f}\n(overall EPA/play: r = {R_ALL_O:.2f})", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK,
        ha="right", va="center", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.4)
plt.show()
```

**Third: no team or coach is reliably a "second-half team."** The right panel of @fig-halftime-test asks
whether improving after halftime is a repeatable trait. If some staffs adjusted better than others, a team
that improved after halftime in one season should tend to do it again the next. It doesn't: the
year-to-year correlation of a team's second-half-minus-first-half EPA per play is
`{python} f"{R_DIFF_O:.2f}"` for offenses and `{python} f"{R_DIFF_D:.2f}"` for defenses, against
`{python} f"{R_ALL_O:.2f}"` and `{python} f"{R_ALL_D:.2f}"` for how good the offense and defense are
overall. Being good carries over from one season to the next; being better after halftime doesn't.

Coaches are the natural place to look next, since a reputation for halftime magic attaches to a person.
@fig-coach-halves plots every head coach with at least 100 games in these seasons by his teams' average
scoring margin in first halves and in second halves.

```{python}
#| label: fig-coach-halves
#| fig-cap: "Head coaches with at least 100 regular-season games, 2006–2025: average scoring margin per game in first halves (x) and in second halves, regulation only (y); bigger dots coached more games. The dashed diagonal is 'just as good after halftime as before.' Good coaches are good in both halves, so the dots rise from left to right. A 'halftime adjuster' would sit well above the diagonal; nobody does by more than about two and a half points a game, a gap that luck alone produces over 100 to 300 games. The two coaches with the best reputations as game planners, Bill Belichick and Andy Reid, sit *below* it: their teams were better before halftime. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.1))
lim = (-3.6, 5.2)
ax.plot(lim, lim, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.7, zorder=1); ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.7, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(COACH["h1"], COACH["h2"], s=COACH["n"] / 6, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.75, lw=0, zorder=3)
label_at = {"Bill Belichick": (-0.5, 0.55), "Andy Reid": (0.25, -0.55), "Sean Payton": (-1.2, 0.55),
            "Pete Carroll": (-1.5, 0.35), "Mike Tomlin": (-0.2, -0.75), "John Harbaugh": (0.3, 0.45),
            "Sean McDermott": (-0.4, 0.62), "Kyle Shanahan": (0.4, -0.6), "Kevin Stefanski": (0.3, -0.45),
            "Mike Shanahan": (-1.1, -0.45)}
for nm, (dx, dy) in label_at.items():
    if nm in COACH.index:
        x, y = COACH.loc[nm, "h1"], COACH.loc[nm, "h2"]
        ax.annotate(nm, (x, y), xytext=(x + dx, y + dy), fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center",
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=3))
ax.text(5.0, -3.0, "dashed line: as good after\nhalftime as before", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="bottom")
ax.set_xlim(*lim); ax.set_ylim(-3.2, 4.8)
ax.set_xlabel("First-half scoring margin per game", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Second-half scoring margin per game", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

So what *does* explain the dots, and the second-half swings fans remember? Three things, and they work at
different scales.

- **Chance, for the coaches.** A coach's second-half-minus-first-half margin over 100 to 300 games still
  wobbles by about a point either way from luck alone (the statistician's "standard error"). Thirty-five
  coaches is a lot of coin-flippers, and you'd expect one or two of them to land more than two of those
  wobbles from zero by chance. That is what @fig-coach-halves shows:
  `{python} f"{(COACH['swing'].abs() < 2 * SWING_SE).sum()}"` of the
  `{python} f"{len(COACH)}"` coaches sit inside that band. Reid's gap is one of the few outside it, which
  is about as many as luck predicts, and if it means anything, it says his teams were unusually good
  *before* halftime, not bad after it.
- **Score effects, for teams that lead.** Teams that lead at halftime play differently afterwards: they
  run more, take fewer risks and drain the clock, while teams that trail throw more and gamble. You can
  see it in @fig-score-effects. A team leading at halftime is usually the better team, so you'd expect it
  to keep outscoring its opponent; instead, leaders by one to 13 points were *outscored* in the second
  half, and big leaders barely broke even. Measured against what their quality predicted, halftime leaders
  gave back about `{python} f"{(SCORE.loc['lead 1-13', 'pred'] - SCORE.loc['lead 1-13', 'h2']):.1f}"`
  points in the second half. That is real, but small next to the dots: even for the coaches who led most
  often, it moves the second-half margin by only about `{python} f"{COACH['score_eff'].abs().max():.1f}"`
  of a point. Score effects change how a game *looks* (more runs, fewer deep shots, a comeback that comes
  up short) far more than they change the final margin.
- **Possessions, for single games.** Second halves start with a kickoff to the team that didn't receive
  the opening one, and most coaches who win the coin toss defer so they get the ball to start the second
  half ([The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)).[^defer]
  In one game that matters: a team that kicked off to start the game, then watched the other offense hold
  the ball for long drives, can come out after halftime with the ball and a fresh set of downs, and look
  like a new team. Over 100 or more games who gets the ball first evens out, so possessions explain
  individual turnarounds like Super Bowl LVII, below, not a coach's dot.

```{python}
#| label: fig-score-effects
#| fig-cap: "Score effects, 2006–2025 regular seasons: second-half scoring margin by halftime score. Light bars are what each team's quality predicted (its average first-half margin in its other games that season, against its opponent's, scaled by how much first halves predict second halves league-wide); dark bars are what actually happened. Leaders, who are usually the better teams, should have kept outscoring their opponents; instead they gave back most of that edge (and trailing teams, necessarily, gained the mirror image). The effect is real but worth well under a point. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 2.6))
xs_ = np.arange(len(SCORE))
ax.bar(xs_ - 0.19, SCORE["pred"], width=0.36, color=style.BASELINE, label="predicted by team quality", zorder=3)
ax.bar(xs_ + 0.19, SCORE["h2"], width=0.36, color=style.SERIES[0], label="actual", zorder=3)
for i, (pv, av) in enumerate(zip(SCORE["pred"], SCORE["h2"])):
    for xx_, v in ((i - 0.19, pv), (i + 0.19, av)):
        ax.text(xx_, v + (0.06 if v >= 0 else -0.06), f"{v:+.1f}", ha="center", va="bottom" if v >= 0 else "top",
                fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, zorder=2)
ax.set_xticks(xs_, [f"{b}\n({n:,} games)" for b, n in zip(["trailing by 14+", "trailing by 1–13", "leading by 1–13",
                                                             "leading by 14+"], SCORE["n"])], fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylim(-1.45, 1.45)
ax.set_ylabel("2nd-half margin (points)", fontsize=7.6)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
ax.legend(fontsize=6.8, loc="upper left", frameon=False)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

None of this means adjustments are fake. Coaches adjust constantly; the between-series loop is real work
that wins plays. The data says something narrower: adjustment is not a *halftime* event that reliably
separates staffs, and a big second-half swing is usually explained by luck, the scoreboard and who had the
ball before you need to credit genius. When a team does turn a game around, look for the specific change.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sb57
#| fig-cap: "Super Bowl LVII by half (runs and passes only). Kansas City's offense ran only 20 plays before halftime to Philadelphia's 44; its EPA per play rose from about +0.15 to about +0.5 (small samples) and its rushing yards from 36 to 126, while its motion rate barely moved. More snaps, a run game and two well-timed calls, not a new motion offense. Sources: nflverse play-by-play; FTN charting (`is_motion`)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(6.6, 2.05))
H = ["Half1", "Half2"]
xl = ["1st", "2nd"]
ax = axes[0]
w = 0.38
for i, (tm, c) in enumerate((("KC", style.SERIES[0]), ("PHI", style.SERIES[1]))):
    vals = [SB.loc[(tm, hh), "snaps"] for hh in H]
    ax.bar(np.arange(2) + (i - 0.5) * w, vals, width=w, color=c, label=tm, zorder=3)
    for j, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax.text(j + (i - 0.5) * w, v + 1, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK)
ax.set_title("Offensive snaps", fontsize=7.8); ax.set_ylim(0, 58)
ax.legend(fontsize=6.2, loc="upper right", handlelength=1.0, borderaxespad=0.2)
for ax, col, ttl, fmt, ylim in ((axes[1], "epa", "KC: EPA per play", "{:+.2f}", (0, 0.7)),
                                (axes[2], "rush_yds", "KC: rushing yards", "{:.0f}", (0, 150)),
                                (axes[3], "motion", "KC: motion rate", "{:.0%}", (0, 0.7))):
    vals = [SB.loc[("KC", hh), col] for hh in H]
    ax.bar(np.arange(2), vals, width=0.55, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3)
    for j, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax.text(j, v + ylim[1] * 0.02, fmt.format(v), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=7.8); ax.set_ylim(*ylim)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks(range(2), xl, fontsize=6.8); ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6.2)
    ax.set_xlabel("half", fontsize=6.6)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[3].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.9)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs, Super Bowl LVII (2022 season)"}
Super Bowl LVII (February 12, 2023) is everyone's favorite example of a halftime turnaround. The Eagles
led 24–14 at the half; Patrick Mahomes had re-aggravated his injured ankle late in the second quarter; and
the Chiefs scored on all four of their second-half possessions to win 38–35, including two fourth-quarter
touchdowns on the same motion play (the story of "Corn Dog" is told in
[Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) and
[What Beats What](08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)).[^sb57] "Kansas City's halftime adjustments" is the
usual summary, and a Super Bowl halftime, stretched for the show, gives a staff far more than the usual 13
minutes to make them. What does the data say changed?


**What to notice:** start with the first panel of @fig-sb57. Kansas City's offense barely played in the first half:
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'snaps']:.0f}"` runs and passes against Philadelphia's
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('PHI', 'Half1'), 'snaps']:.0f}"`, because the Eagles' offense held the ball for long
drives. The Chiefs had been effective when they did have it, about
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'epa']:+.2f}"` EPA per play, and the second half gave them
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half2'), 'snaps']:.0f}"` snaps, starting with the ball: Philadelphia had
received the opening kickoff, so Kansas City received the second-half kickoff and drove for a touchdown.
That is the possessions effect in a single game. Some of the change was real and visible: the
run game went from `{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'rush_yds']:.0f}"` rushing yards to
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half2'), 'rush_yds']:.0f}"`, with Isiah Pacheco and Jerick McKinnon running
well and Mahomes scrambling on the bad ankle. What *didn't*
change much was the motion: by FTN's charting the Chiefs used motion on
`{python} pct(SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'motion'])` of first-half snaps and
`{python} pct(SB.loc[('KC', 'Half2'), 'motion'])` after halftime.[^ftn] The two motion touchdowns were a
game-plan call used at the right moment near the goal line (the second one set up by Kadarius Toney's
65-yard punt return, the longest in Super Bowl history), not a new offense invented in the locker room.

One thing held in *both* halves. Philadelphia's defense led the league with
`{python} f"{PHI_SACKS22:.0f}"` sacks in the 2022 regular season and sacked Mahomes
`{python} "zero times" if SB_SACKS == 0 else f"{SB_SACKS:.0f} times"` in the Super Bowl, even on a bad
ankle. Kansas City's protection plan, built during the week, worked from the first snap. And
Philadelphia's offense didn't collapse after halftime: it ran
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('PHI', 'Half2'), 'snaps']:.0f}"` plays at a *better* EPA per play
(`{python} f"{SB.loc[('PHI', 'Half2'), 'epa']:+.2f}"`, up from
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('PHI', 'Half1'), 'epa']:+.2f}"`), and scored 11 points. The Eagles lost the
second half because their defense, after keeping the Chiefs' offense off the field for most of the first
half, couldn't get a single stop.

So was it halftime adjustments? Partly: the Chiefs ran more and ran better, and the staff saved its best
red-zone call for the moments that mattered. But the honest summary also includes the second-half
kickoff, a punt return, a protection plan that never needed adjusting, and an Eagles defense that simply
didn't stop anything. (If anyone's defense was worn down, it was Kansas City's, which had been on the
field for 44 first-half plays.) That's the habit this chapter wants you to build: when someone credits
halftime, ask what changed, and check how much of it was the clock and the bounces.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the adjustment hunter"}
Pick one team for a game and keep a short list in two columns, first half and second half.

**Before the snap**

- **Personnel:** which groups does the offense use, and does the defense still match them? A team that
  lived in 11 personnel and comes out in 12 has changed its plan.
- **Tempo:** does the offense go fast after big plays? Does the defense look rushed, with players running
  off at the snap or a plain, undisguised look?
- **Motion:** more or less of it after halftime, and does the defense still follow it the same way?
- **Coverage shell:** two-high or one-high before the snap, and does it change after the half?

**After the snap**

- **Pressure:** count rushers on third down in each half. Did a blitz that worked disappear, or one that
  got burned stop coming?
- **Protection:** is a back or tight end staying in to help a struggling tackle after halftime?
- **The fix and the answer:** when the defense changes something, watch the next series. Does the offense
  call the play that beats the change? That's the call after the call.

Then check the box score: who had more snaps in each half, and who led at halftime? Before you credit an
adjustment, ask whether the scoreboard and the clock explain the second half.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: one fresh receiver"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sub
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10, second quarter. On the previous snap the offense, in 12 personnel with both tight ends attached, gained 19 yards on a play-action pass, and the defense was in base personnel (three linebackers). The offense wants to keep the pace up and attack those linebackers with receivers, so as it hustles to the line its tired second tight end (U, purple ring) jogs off and a third wide receiver (H) runs on to the slot. The quarterback is in the shotgun waving everyone into place, and the defense's nickel back is standing on its sideline."
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.0, "R"),
                O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.0, "H"),
                O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.0, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 14.0, "Z"), O("U", "TE", -7.5, -12.6, "U")]
p = Play(off, base_vs_flexed(False), los=50, to_go=None)
p.highlight("U", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 17.5), window=(-10.6, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
ghost(f, p, [(-4.6, -16.6), (-2.8, -11.5), (-1.9, -8.9)], color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.8, lw=1.5)
ghost(f, p, [(-7.3, -11.4), (-7.6, -16.4)], color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.8, lw=1.5)
say(f, p, -4.6, -12.6, "H running on", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, -8.9, -9.3, "U jogging off", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, 13.4, 1.8, "base: 3 LBs\n(nickel on the sideline)", fontsize=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**The offense wants to snap fast and throw at those linebackers. What happens before the snap, and what
matchup will the offense actually get?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The substitution kills the tempo. Because the offense changed a player, the umpire stands over the ball
until the defense has had time to answer, and the defense sends its nickel on for a linebacker. The offense
gets three receivers against a nickel defense: the ordinary matchup, not the one it wanted.** The rule
doesn't care that it was only one player, or that the offense was in a hurry: *any* offensive substitution
before the two-minute warning opens the defense's window. If the quarterback snaps while the umpire is
still over the ball, the first time costs a warning and a replayed down, and after that 15 yards.

Compare @fig-freeze. There the offense kept the same eleven and *moved* its tight ends into the slots
instead of swapping one for a receiver, and the defense was stuck with linebackers on them. Same goal, and
the difference is one player crossing the sideline. That is the cost listed earlier, "your own
substitutions get harder," in action: the tired tight end has to stay on the field if the offense wants
the freeze, which is why tempo teams prize tight ends who can block *and* run routes, and why they pick
the moments they go fast. (Why sub here at all? Maybe U was gassed, or hurt, or the coach simply wanted his
receiver more than he wanted the freeze. Sometimes that's the right trade.)

If the defense, for its own reasons, *doesn't* bring the nickel on, the offense gets exactly what it
wanted: H, a receiver, against a linebacker in the slot. That is the throw.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the call after the call"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sit
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6, third quarter. Same offense, same 2x2 formation as in the first half, when mesh (two shallow crossers) beat the defense's man coverage three times. Since halftime the defense has shown the same single-high look, but its two inside defenders (purple rings) now sit at five to six yards and pass the crossers off to each other, and it has stopped three straight crossing plays. The dashed circles show where those two defenders sat on those plays, waiting for whichever crosser came to them."
p = Play(spread(), cover1_look(), los=62, to_go=6)
p.highlight("NB", "SS", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-16.5, 16.5), window=(-8.6, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
for spot in ((6.3, -5.4), (4.9, 5.4)):     # where the two sat on the crossing plays since halftime
    x_, y_ = _P(f, p, *spot)
    f.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x_), float(y_)), 1.9, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0,
                          ls=(0, (3, 2)), alpha=0.6, zorder=4))
point_to(f, p, (10.8, -2.0), (6.3, -5.4), "since halftime: sit here,\ntake whoever comes", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**The offense has seen the adjustment. What does it call now, and who is it aimed at?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A route that uses the sitting defenders' new habit against them: most likely a pivot (whip) route by a slot
receiver, or a crosser that keeps climbing behind them, with the target being the space the sitter just
committed to leave.** The second-half rule tells each inside defender to stop at five or six yards and take
whoever comes into his area. A slot receiver who runs straight at that defender as if he's crossing, then
plants and snaps back the way he came, is working against a man who has just committed to the cross; the
defender is standing still and has to turn and chase. Many offenses pair it with a crosser from the other
side that, instead of flattening at five yards, keeps climbing to eight or ten, behind the sitters and in
front of the deep safety.

This is the call after the call: the offense isn't trying to beat the first-half man coverage any more,
and it isn't simply running mesh again. It's punishing the specific way the defense fixed mesh. Expect the
defense to answer that, too, perhaps by mixing the man coverage back in so the sitters can't be read in
advance. Another good answer is the running back: a back who releases late on a wheel or rail route up the
sideline is running away from defenders who are looking inside for crossers. If you said "run the ball,"
that's reasonable partial credit: two defenders standing at five yards looking for crossers are a step
slower to the run, but on third-and-6 most play-callers would rather attack the adjustment directly.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: no waiting"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sugar
#| fig-cap: "Fourth-and-1 near midfield, early in the fourth quarter. On third down the offense was stopped a yard short. Instead of waiting, it has gathered in a tight huddle about five yards behind the ball, with the same players who were on the field for third down: three tight ends (Y, U and V) and a fullback (F). The defense still has its base personnel out there; its heavier short-yardage group is on its sideline. The play clock shows 35."
huddle = []
names = [("QB", "QB", "Q"), ("C", "C", "C"), ("LG", "LG", ""), ("RG", "RG", ""), ("LT", "LT", ""), ("RT", "RT", ""),
         ("RB", "RB", "R"), ("FB", "FB", "F"), ("Y", "TE", "Y"), ("U", "TE", "U"), ("V", "TE", "V")]
for i, (k_, pos_, lab) in enumerate(names):
    a_ = 2 * np.pi * i / len(names) + np.pi / 2
    huddle.append(O(k_, pos_, -4.8 + 2.2 * np.cos(a_), 2.9 * np.sin(a_), lab))
p = Play(huddle, base_vs_tight(), los=58, to_go=1)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-9.6, 15.5), width_in=5.4)
say(f, p, -5.0, 8.4, "tight huddle\nabout 5 yards back", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, 10.2, -5.0, "base defense still on;\nshort-yardage group\non the sideline", fontsize=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**What is the offense trying to do, and when? Then switch sides: you are the defensive coordinator. Do you
call a timeout, and what does each choice cost you?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**It's a sugar huddle, and the offense wants to snap before the defense can get its short-yardage personnel
on the field or set its own call: expect a fast snap, with twenty-five or more seconds still on the play
clock, and a short-yardage run, most likely a quarterback sneak or an inside run behind the extra tight
ends.** The huddle lets the offense give a precise call to everyone at once (no signals for the defense to
steal) and still get to the line almost immediately. Because the offense already has its heavy personnel on
the field from third down and isn't substituting now, the umpire won't stand over the ball for the
defense: if the defense starts sending in its goal-line players, it risks being caught with twelve on the
field.

**The defense's choice.** *No timeout:* play the down with the base players on the field and a simple
short-yardage call (everyone low, fill the gaps). It keeps the timeout for the end of the game, but it is
defending fourth-and-1 with lighter players than it wants. *Timeout:* it gets its short-yardage group on and
a proper call in, but it spends one of its three second-half timeouts with a quarter to play, and it gives
the offense the same minute to think, change its play or bring on its own short-yardage specialists. On a
fourth down near midfield the timeout is often worth spending, because the down is worth more than the
timeout; skipping it makes sense for a defense that trusts its call. Either way the sugar huddle has already won something:
it has forced the defense to choose.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Adjusting is constant and small.** Between series, the booth's tallies and the tablet photos meet the
  coaches and players on the bench, and what comes out is a rule, an alignment, a protection call or a
  re-ranked call sheet, chosen from plays already practiced.
- **Tempo is a weapon about the rules, not just speed.** The defense may match personnel only when the
  offense substitutes, so an offense that keeps its eleven and goes fast freezes the defense in the wrong
  players, tires it, and strips away its disguise. The sugar huddle gets the same benefits with a huddle's
  clarity.
- **Tempo costs the offense too.** Few personnel groups, simple calls, tired players and, above all, its own
  defense back on the field after a fast three-and-out. Kelly's Eagles were the fastest offense in the
  league for three seasons and their defense faced the most plays each year.
- **Tempo works, a little, as a change-up.** Fast snaps gain about three hundredths of a point of EPA per
  play more than slow ones in the same situation, at the moments play-callers choose them. That is why
  the league tried going fast all game in the mid-2010s and then went back to using it in spots.
- **Defenses answer tempo by being sound rather than clever:** substituting at the whistle, one-word calls,
  rules the players finish themselves, and versatile players who never need to come off. Each has a
  price. The league polices the rest.
- **The call after the call** is choosing the play that beats the defense's *next* answer. Watch the series
  after a team fixes something.
- **"Halftime adjustments" mostly don't survive the data as a decisive, repeatable skill.** First and second
  halves look the same league-wide, bad halves regress to the mean, being better after halftime doesn't carry
  over from season to season, and luck, the scoreboard and who had the ball explain most big swings. Ask
  what changed.

    and the league's own page, updated for the 2025 switch to Surface Copilot+ PCs, still describes images only.

[^halftime]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 1, Article 3: "Between the second and third periods, there shall be an

    for the show.

[^playclock]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 6, Article 1 (the 40-second play clock, which starts when a play ends)
    and Article 2 (a 25-second clock after certain administrative stoppages):
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^tempodata]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`game_seconds_remaining`), regular seasons. A pair of
    snaps counts when both are runs or passes on the same drive and quarter, nothing else is logged between them, the
    earlier play was a run or a completed pass that did not go out of bounds and had no penalty, timeout, touchdown,
    lost fumble or spike, both snaps came with win probability between 20% and 80%, and the earlier snap came with more
    than 2:30 left in the half (so the two-minute warning and the late-half out-of-bounds clock rules can't interfere).
    Gaps under 5 or over 60 seconds are dropped as clock errors. The number includes the duration of the earlier play
    (usually 4–7 seconds), so it is not the same as time left on the play clock; nflverse's `play_clock` field is not
    usable for this. The 30-second threshold is this chapter's choice.

[^subrule]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 5, Section 2, Article 10 ("If a substitution is made by the offense before the
    two-minute warning of either half, the offense shall not be permitted to snap the ball until the defense has been
    permitted to respond with its substitutions"; "The Umpire will stand over the ball until the Referee deems that the
    defense has had a reasonable time to complete its substitutions"; a first violation brings a warning and a replay of
    the down, later ones a 15-yard unsportsmanlike conduct foul) and Article 11 (simulated substitutions):
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^defer]: The option to defer was added in 2008; coin-toss winners deferred 8% of the time in 2008 and 76% in the first half

    and about five times in six by 2018 (Zach Barnett, FootballScoop, Sept. 7, 2018:
    <https://footballscoop.com/news/number-nfl-coaches-deferring-kickoff-skyrocketed-past-decade>).

[^tmm]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2016–2025: accepted or declined fouls logged as

    `no_huddle` flag. Rates: `{python} f"{TMM_RATE.loc[1.0]:.1f}"` per 1,000 no-huddle snaps against
    `{python} f"{TMM_RATE.loc[0.0]:.1f}"` per 1,000 other snaps. Rule 5, Section 1 of the NFL Rulebook (2026) makes
    twelve or more defenders in the formation with the snap imminent a dead-ball foul, and twelve or more on the
    field at the snap a live-ball foul: <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^tempowork]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2006–2025, using the running-clock snap pairs
    described in the note on the tempo chart. "Same down and distance" compares fast and slower snaps within each
    down and distance band (1–2, 3–5, 6–9, 10, 11–15 and 16+ yards to go) and weights the differences by how often
    fast snaps occur in each band. Success rate is the share of plays with positive EPA, as in nflverse.

[^pffmotion]: Daire Carragher, "NFL pre-snap motion usage reaches new highs across the NFL," PFF (Feb. 23, 2026), pre-snap
    shift or motion rate by season: <https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-pre-snap-motion-usage-reaches-new-highs-across-the-nfl>.
    PFF's definition differs from the FTN `is_motion` flag used later in this chapter, so the two series aren't comparable.

[^dlsnaps]: Course calculation from Pro Football Reference snap counts via nflverse (`load_snap_counts`), 2025 regular
    season: players listed as DE, DT, NT or DL with at least ten games, each player's average share of his team's
    defensive snaps. Many edge rushers in 3-4 defenses are listed as linebackers and aren't counted.

[^replay]: "Replay review in gridiron football," Wikipedia: in the NFL, scoring plays (since 2011) and turnovers (since
    2012) are reviewed only at the replay official's initiative, and "a questionable call may not be challenged
    once the next play is underway, so coaches may be forced to make a quick decision without the benefit of seeing
    a replay": <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Replay_review_in_gridiron_football>. The details of who may initiate a
    review, and of the replay assist added in 2025, are in the NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 15:
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^phi13]: Pro Football Reference, 2013 Philadelphia Eagles (10–6, first in the NFC East; LeSean McCoy led the league in
    rushing): <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/phi/2013.htm>. In this course's nflverse count the Eagles also
    led all teams in rushing yards that season.

[^kellydata]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2013–2015, runs and passes (scrambles and
    sacks counted as passes; two-point tries excluded). Offensive rank is by EPA per play among 32 teams. Tempo numbers
    use the method in the note on the tempo chart.

[^giants11]: Associated Press, "NFL memo warns teams on faking injuries" (Sept. 21, 2011), after Deon Grant and Jacquian
    Williams went down against the Rams' no-huddle; the memo warned of "fines, suspensions and loss of draft picks":
    <https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2011/sep/21/nfl-memo-warns-teams-on-faking-injuries/>. Grant denied faking.

[^injury]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 5, Article 3 (injury timeouts before the two-minute warning: "the
    injured player must leave the game for the completion of one down," with exceptions):
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^ncaa10]: *Sports Illustrated*, "NCAA proposes rule change to allow time for defensive substitutions" (Feb. 12, 2014),
    on the proposal that offenses could not snap until 29 seconds remained on the play clock, outside the last two
    minutes of each half: <https://www.si.com/college/2014/02/12/ncaa-rule-change-defensive-substitutions-targeting>.
    The rules committee tabled it on March 5, 2014, before the Playing Rules Oversight Panel could vote on it: Associated
    Press, "NCAA tables 10-second football rule proposal," *Bangor Daily News* (March 5, 2014):
    <https://www.bangordailynews.com/2014/03/05/sports/ncaa-tables-10-second-football-rule-proposal/>.

[^halfdata]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2006–2025. Snaps are runs and passes with a
    down recorded, more than two minutes left in the half and win probability between 10% and 90%. A team-game is kept if
    the offense had at least 15 such snaps in the first half and 10 in the second. Season-to-season correlations pair
    each team with itself the next season (608 pairs). The coach chart uses actual scores at the end of the second and
    fourth quarters (overtime excluded) and each game's listed head coach; coaches with at least 100 games in these
    seasons are shown. Under pure chance, the standard error of a coach's second-half-minus-first-half margin over a few
    hundred games is about 0.5–1 point, so differences of up to about 2 points are unremarkable.

[^sb57]: "Super Bowl LVII," Wikipedia (Kansas City 38, Philadelphia 35, Feb. 12, 2023; 24–14 Philadelphia at
    halftime): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII>; *Sports Illustrated*, "Patrick Mahomes Reinjures Ankle in
    Second Quarter of Super Bowl LVII" (Feb. 13, 2023):
    <https://www.si.com/nfl/2023/02/13/patrick-mahomes-reinjures-ankle-second-quarter-super-bowl-lvii>; Chiefs.com,
    "Kadarius Toney Comes Through in a Big Way as Part of Record-Setting Super Bowl" (65-yard punt return, the longest in
    Super Bowl history): <https://www.chiefs.com/news/kadarius-toney-comes-through-in-a-big-way-as-part-of-record-setting-super-bowl>.
    Snap counts, EPA and rushing yards by half are a course calculation from nflverse play-by-play.

[^ftn]: FTN charting via nflverse (`load_ftn_charting`), whose `is_motion` flag means motion occurred on the play before
    *or at* the snap: <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html>. It is not comparable with
    PFF's shift-and-motion series.
